sources.title: Nanite: A Deep Dive (SIGGRAPH 2021, Advances in Real-Time Rendering in Games)
sources.author_or_publisher: Brian Karis, Rune Stubbe, Graham Wihlidal (Epic Games)
sources.locator: Slides: p.16 'Triangle cluster culling'; p.17 'Occlusion culling' (test against lowest HZB mip where screen rect <= 4x4); p.28 'Cluster hierarchy'; p.44 'Explicit dependency / Quick-VDR / Batched Multi-Triangulation'; p.47 'DAG'; p.49 METIS graph partitioning; p.67 'Seamless LOD' (if < 1 pixel error, no transition needed); p.70 'Hierarchical culling'; p.73 'Persistent Threads - Hierarchy Culling'; p.81 'Software Rasterization' (3x faster); p.88 'Clusters with edges <32 pixels are SW rasterized'; p.95 'Tiny instances'; p.96 '10M * float4x3 = 457MB'; p.97 'Visibility buffer imposters' (12x12 view directions, 12x12 pixels per direction, 8:8 Depth+TriangleID, 40.5KB per mesh); p.115 'Virtual shadow maps' (16k x 16k); p.116 'Page size = 128 x 128'; p.125 'Group parts' (clusters ~2KB, groups 8-32 clusters, 128KB page, ~1KB average slack per page); p.126 'Deciding what to stream'; p.134 'Memory - Triangles and attributes' (~17 bits per triangle, octahedral normals, implicit tangents 0 bits); p.138 'GPU transcoding' (~50GB/s on PS5); p.140 '~30% of vertices coded as references'; p.142 '~5 bits/tri vs ~17 bits/tri'; p.144 'Results: Lumen in the Land of Nanite' (433M input -> 882M Nanite triangles; raw 25.90GB; memory format 7.67GB; compressed 6.77GB; compressed disk 4.61GB; 5.6 bytes per Nanite triangle; 11.4 bytes per input triangle; 1M triangles = ~10.9MB on disk); p.145 'Compressed sizes are on PC using Kraken at Compression Level 5'; p.146 'Future' (no translucent/masked, no non-rigid deformation, not great with aggregates)
sources.applicability_note: The single richest primary source for virtual geometry, GPU culling, clusters, impostors and geometry compression, with measured/published numbers. Caveat: the byte-size results are for one specific Epic demo scene compressed with Kraken level 5; they are not a general ratio. The 3x software-rasterizer figure and the 50 GB/s transcode figure are measured on the hardware stated on the slide (PS5 for transcoding).

sources.title: GPU-Driven Rendering Pipelines (SIGGRAPH 2015, Advances in Real-Time Rendering in Games)
sources.author_or_publisher: Ulrich Haar (Ubisoft Montreal), Sebastian Aaltonen (RedLynx, Ubisoft)
sources.engine_or_api_version: DirectX 11 (console) + DX12 notes; Assassin's Creed Unity / RedLynx in-house engine
sources.locator: Slides: p.9 AC Unity '~10x instances compared to previous Assassin's Creed games'; p.10 'Mesh Cluster Rendering' (fixed topology 64 vertex strip); p.12 '64 triangles per cluster'; p.13 pipeline diagram (MULTI-DRAW -> INSTANCE CULLING -> CLUSTER CHUNK EXPANSION -> CLUSTER CULLING -> INDEX BUFFER COMPACTION); p.22-24 'Static Triangle Backface Culling' ('10-30% triangles culled'); p.26-27 'Occlusion Depth Generation' (300 best occluders ~600us; downsample to 512x256 100us; reprojection 50us; depth hierarchy 50us; PS4 performance); p.37 'Results' (CPU: 1-2 orders of magnitude fewer drawcalls, ~75% of previous AC CPU with ~10x objects; GPU: 20-40% triangles culled, 'only small overall gain: <10% of geometry rendering', 30-80% shadow triangles culled); p.40 'Virtual Texturing' (virtual 256k^2 texel atlas, 128^2 texel pages, 8k^2 texture page cache, 5-slice array, BC5/BC3); p.42 'Single Draw Call Rendering' (+2% cost for dynamic branching); p.44 'Virtual Deferred Texturing' (16+16 bit UV to 8k^2 atlas); p.50 '8xMSAA Trick Benchmark' (G-buffer 3.03 ms -> 2.06 ms, -32%; pixel shader waves -55%; DRAM 76.3 MB -> 60.9 MB, -20%); p.53-54 'Benchmark' (250,000 separate moving objects, 1 GB of mesh data, 10k+ meshes, 8k^2 texture cache atlas, only two DrawInstancedIndirect calls; GPU total 2.3 ms; CPU 0.2 ms on a single Jaguar core; Xbox One, 1080p); p.55 'Virtual Shadow Mapping' (128k^2 virtual shadow map, 256^2 texel pages); p.56 'Measured: Up to 3.5x faster than SDSM in complex sparse scenes; slightly slower than SDSM & CSM in simple scenes'
sources.applicability_note: Primary source with measured CPU/GPU results for GPU-driven cluster culling and two-phase occlusion on 2015-era console hardware. Transfer warning: the absolute ms figures are for Xbox One / PS4 at 1080p in 2015; only the ratios and the 'small overall gain' conclusion are informative for modern PC.

sources.author_or_publisher: Arul Asirvatham and Hugues Hoppe (NVIDIA / Microsoft Research), Addison-Wesley

world_partition_streaming.problem: A world larger than a few square kilometres cannot be resident in memory, cannot be lit/collision-built as one unit, and cannot be edited by more than a handful of people at once. The classic UE answer (persistent level + hand-placed sublevels + streaming volumes) pushes the whole spatial problem onto designers, who must hand-author load/unload volumes, keep them in sync with the art, and resolve file conflicts on the single .umap. Runtime streaming also needs a decision procedure: which cells to load, at what range, in what priority, and what to do about actors that must exist everywhere. World Partition replaces hand-authored volumes with a spatial hash grid plus streaming sources, and replaces the monolithic map file with one file per actor so that cell granularity is a data property rather than an authoring burden.

implementation_variants.name: Runtime spatial hash grid with streaming sources (default)
implementation_variants.description: The world is partitioned into a 2D runtime hash grid; cells are loaded/unloaded around registered streaming sources (player, or an explicit World Partition Streaming Source component). Epic's documentation example uses a 256 m cell with a 768 m loading range; if a streaming source has no explicit shape, it uses a sphere whose radius equals the grid loading range.

implementation_variants.name: Distance + angle importance weighting to bound cell count
implementation_variants.description: Cell importance is not pure distance: wp.Runtime.RuntimeSpatialHashCellToSourceAngleContributionToCellImportance (0..1) modulates how much the angle between the source's view direction and the cell contributes, so cells behind the player are deprioritised and the number of live cells at a given range drops.

implementation_variants.name: Multiple named grids / Data Layers over one world
implementation_variants.description: Actors can be assigned to Data Layers and to runtime grids whose state is toggled at runtime, so a single spatial hash can carry several independently activated sets (e.g. a quest state, a season, a destroyed variant) without duplicating geometry. Epic warns that using more than one grid can negatively impact performance, so this is a per-need tool, not a default.

implementation_variants.name: One File Per Actor as the authoring substrate (editor-only)
implementation_variants.description: Each actor is stored in its own external file so that cell content can be streamed and versioned per actor. Critical caveat: OFPA is an editor-only representation - all actors are embedded back into their level files at cook time, so it changes collaboration and cook behaviour, not runtime file granularity (that is the IoStore/pak layer, see build_size_startup_budgets).

implementation_variants.name: Commandlet-driven bulk processing (conversion, HLOD, minimap)
implementation_variants.description: World Partition ships WorldPartitionBuilder commandlets (conversion, HLOD build, minimap) so that grid/LOD state can be regenerated in CI rather than by opening the editor. This is what makes a partitioned world maintainable at scale.

world_partition_streaming.applicability_conditions: Any world whose content cannot be fully resident, or where more than a few people edit the same map concurrently, or where the camera can move continuously over long distances. Requires actors that are Static or otherwise safe to load/unload (mobility and 'is spatially contained in a cell' become load-bearing facts). Requires the cook/packaging step to understand the partitioned world (it does, via the commandlets).
world_partition_streaming.limitations: Cell size and loading range are coupled: at a fixed loading range, halving the cell size roughly quadruples the number of candidate cells. Very large single actors (a long bridge, a river spline, a Landscape) do not fit neatly into a cell and need special handling or a separate grid. Anything that must be globally consistent (navmesh, gameplay state, AI that roams) has to be reconciled across cell boundaries. OFPA multiplies file count, and Epic warns that a user can check out many files and submit only some, leaving dangling references. Using more than one runtime grid has a documented performance cost.
world_partition_streaming.required_data_and_tools: A world whose actors have sane bounds; a runtime grid configuration (cell size, loading range, grid count); streaming sources registered for every camera-like entity (including cinematics and spectator views); the World Partition window/visualiser for debugging; the builder commandlets wired into CI.

impact.cpu: low to medium - per-frame source/cell evaluation replaces per-frame level-streaming volume tests, and it removes the render-thread cost of keeping the whole world's primitives registered
impact.gpu: none directly; it changes what is submitted, not how it is drawn
impact.ram: high positive - resident actor set is bounded by the streaming range instead of by world size
impact.vram: medium positive - fewer resident textures/meshes; the residual is dominated by HLOD and shared assets
impact.disk: neutral to negative - OFPA increases file count in the editor (cooked output is unaffected); random-read patterns increase
impact.network: none unless the world is server-authoritative

world_partition_streaming.quality_impact: Neutral by construction, negative if mistuned: too small a loading range produces visible pop-in and missing collision; too large negates the memory saving. The visual quality of the far field is the job of hierarchical_lod, not of the partitioner.
world_partition_streaming.concept_impact: Unlocks world sizes and team sizes that are otherwise unreachable, and makes 'open world' a setting rather than an engine fork. It also makes the streaming range an explicit, tunable design parameter, which is a design constraint (encounter spacing, travel speed) as much as a technical one.
world_partition_streaming.recommended_stage: preproduction; the grid, cell size and OFPA/source-control workflow must exist before content is authored at volume, because retrofitting them means re-saving every actor.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 4d grid/loading-range configuration and profiling + 4d conversion of existing levels and OFPA source-control workflow + 4d streaming-source integration for all camera-like entities + 3d CI commandlets + 3d pop-in/load-hitch debugging across the world; p80 adds a second runtime grid or Data Layer scheme and a landscape/river special case

relations.note: HLOD is what makes unloaded World Partition cells still visible; the two are documented as one system.
Cell streaming is only as smooth as the background loader behind it; partition without async IO just moves the hitch.
Cell streaming produces exactly the many-small-reads workload DirectStorage targets.
Both address 'the world is bigger than the engine's comfortable coordinates'; partitioning bounds residency, origin shifting bounds precision. A very large world needs both.
OFPA's editor file explosion is separate from cook size; teams frequently conflate the two and mis-diagnose build-size regressions.

world_partition_streaming.verification: Enable the runtime-hash debug draw (wp.Runtime.ToggleDrawRuntimeHash2D / 3D), fly the world at maximum travel speed and record: max concurrently loaded cells, load/unload event count per second, and any frame where a cell's actors appear without collision. Then measure resident memory with the streaming range at its shipping value and at 1.5x, and confirm the delta matches the predicted cell count. Finally, run the HLOD commandlet in CI and diff the generated actor set between runs.

world_origin_shifting.problem: Single-precision floats distribute their ~7 decimal digits around zero, so at large world coordinates the representable spacing grows: vertex jitter, quantised animation, broken physics contacts, and Z-fighting all appear far from the origin even though the content itself is fine. This is independent of streaming - it is purely a function of coordinate magnitude. The two families of answer are (a) make the coordinate type wider (double precision / LWC), and (b) keep the numbers small by moving the origin so that active content is always near zero (origin rebasing / camera-relative rendering).

implementation_variants.name: Large World Coordinates: widen the type to double (Epic's shipped answer)
implementation_variants.description: UE5 LWC introduces double-precision variants of core types across the engine, Niagara, Chaos and HLSL. Gameplay/CPU transforms become doubles; the GPU still receives camera-relative positions, so shaders do not pay for 64-bit maths. Epic's default WORLD_MAX becomes 88 million km, with UE_USE_UE4_WORLD_MAX in EngineDefines.h restored to the old 21 km if wanted.

implementation_variants.name: Origin rebasing / shifting (the classic and still-valid answer)
implementation_variants.description: Keep floats but periodically translate the world (or the camera-relative frame) so the active region sits near zero. Godot's documentation states the trade-off plainly: 'On low-end platforms, an origin shifting approach can be used instead to allow for large worlds without using' double precision. This is the option to pick when doubles are too expensive or unavailable (mobile, console memory budgets, third-party middleware that assumes float).

implementation_variants.name: Split representation for particle systems
implementation_variants.description: Where doubles are unaffordable per-particle, store a float position within a grid cell plus the cell index. UE's Niagara does exactly this: 'the data is stored as a set of floats instead of using doubles... the first float then defines the Niagara system in that grid cell, and the second represents which grid cell the system is in', exposed as a new Position type.

implementation_variants.name: Camera-relative shader translation (mandatory companion)
implementation_variants.description: Regardless of CPU precision, positions must reach the GPU relative to the view origin; this is the mechanism that lets LWC avoid double-precision shader maths. Any custom HLSL that ignores it will silently lose the benefit - UE provides LargeWorldCoordinates.ush helpers for that migration.

world_origin_shifting.applicability_conditions: Worlds whose playable extent is larger than roughly 10-20 km with float transforms, or any project that sees jitter/contact artefacts at the far corners. If you are on UE5 and can accept a Beta-flagged engine feature, LWC is the lower-effort route; if you target platforms where doubles are costly, or you use middleware that hard-assumes float, rebasing is the correct route. Both require that no gameplay system stores absolute world coordinates in a durable save without a frame of reference.
world_origin_shifting.limitations: Epic explicitly marks LWC as a Beta feature and says 'use caution when shipping with it'. Doubles double transform memory and can cost CPU throughput in tight loops. Rebasing introduces a discrete event: everything holding absolute positions must be notified and corrected at the same instant, or you get a visible teleport; physics contacts and in-flight particles are the usual breakage. Neither approach fixes shader-side precision for techniques that need absolute world position (world-space noise, triplanar projection, large-scale world-position-offset animation) - those need authoring workarounds. Chaos and Niagara each have their own partial story.
world_origin_shifting.required_data_and_tools: An inventory of every absolute-coordinate consumer (save games, minimap, navmesh, audio, replication, editor tooling); a rebasing event with a single authority; a way to test at the world's far corner (a teleport-to-corner test map); and, if going the LWC route, a full audit of UFUNCTIONs exposing float (Epic warns these 'risk introducing imprecision').

impact.cpu: low for rebasing (rare event, O(live objects)); medium for LWC (doubles cost memory bandwidth and some ALU in transform-heavy CPU code)
impact.gpu: low - LWC is designed so shaders keep receiving camera-relative floats; no 64-bit shader maths
impact.ram: medium negative for LWC - double transforms roughly double that memory; rebasing has no such cost
impact.vram: none directly

impact.network: medium negative - replicated transforms get wider; quantisation or relative-frame replication becomes necessary

world_origin_shifting.quality_impact: Directly positive at distance: removes vertex jitter and physics breakdown. Neutral near the origin. If rebasing is mistimed the artefact is a visible hitch, which is worse than the jitter it fixes.
world_origin_shifting.concept_impact: Sets the hard ceiling on world size, and therefore on the kinds of game you can ship. It is also the constraint that most often surprises teams late, because it is invisible in a small test map.
world_origin_shifting.recommended_stage: preproduction; it is a data-model decision. Retrofitting doubles or rebasing after content and save formats exist is one of the most expensive late changes available in engine work.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3d decision + precision audit of all absolute-coordinate consumers + 4d implementation (LWC conversion or rebasing event) + 3d corner-of-world test map and physics/particle fix-up + 2d replication/save-format review; p80 adds third-party middleware that cannot be recompiled and per-system shader fixes

relations.note: Partitioning bounds what is resident; origin handling bounds how precisely it can be placed. Independent problems that both scale with world extent.
Clipmap/terrain LOD schemes centre on the viewer; an origin shift changes the centre and must be applied to the terrain frame in the same event or the terrain will visibly jump.
Distance-field/global-distance-field volumes are camera-following clipmaps; a rebasing event that moves the camera discretely invalidates their cached update region.
Chunked generation keys content by absolute chunk coordinate; rebasing must not change the chunk key or the same chunk will regenerate differently.

world_origin_shifting.verification: Build a test map at the maximum intended coordinate magnitude (or teleport there), then: (1) look for vertex jitter while the camera is stationary; (2) stack physics bodies and check for contact instability; (3) run a particle system with world-space spawn positions and check for quantised stepping; (4) if rebasing, trigger a rebase while recording and scrub for a one-frame position discontinuity of any object; (5) round-trip a save game across the shift.

hierarchical_lod.problem: Once a world is partitioned, distant cells are unloaded - which is exactly where the player is looking. HLOD replaces the contents of an unloaded cell (or a group of cells) with a single cheap proxy: one mesh, one material, one draw call, possibly instanced. Without it, streaming produces a world whose horizon is empty, and the only alternative - raising the loading range until distant cells stay resident - defeats the point of streaming. HLOD is the bridge between 'load less' and 'see just as far'.

implementation_variants.name: Instancing layer (best for foliage and repeated props)
implementation_variants.description: Static meshes in the layer are replaced by Instanced Static Mesh components using the lowest LOD of each asset. Epic states this type 'is ideal for imposter meshes, such as trees and foliage' - it keeps per-asset identity, so it is also the cheapest to rebuild.

implementation_variants.name: Merged Mesh layer (one proxy mesh, no simplification)
implementation_variants.description: All static meshes in the cell are merged into a single proxy mesh with a baked-flat material. Settings include target lightmap resolution, gutter size, texture binning, landscape culling ('Uses available landscape geometry to cull invisible triangles'), and 'Allow Distance Fields' which can be disabled purely to save memory for a distant-only proxy.

implementation_variants.name: Simplified Mesh layer (merge + geometric simplification)
implementation_variants.description: Merge plus real mesh simplification with a screen-size target: Screen Size, Merge Distance (which 'can close gaps like doors and windows in distant geometry'), Hard Edge Angle, Normal Calculation Method (angle/area/equal weighted), and even collision generation. This is the highest-fidelity and most expensive-to-build variant.

implementation_variants.name: Parent layers / cascaded HLOD
implementation_variants.description: A Parent Layer lets one HLOD layer's output feed another, giving a cascade (near HLOD -> far HLOD -> always-loaded skyline). This is how you avoid a single proxy resolution that is too detailed for the far field and too coarse for the mid field.

implementation_variants.name: Always Loaded layers for the horizon
implementation_variants.description: Setting Always Loaded removes the Cell Size / Loading Range options entirely and keeps the proxy permanently resident - the correct treatment for a skyline or distant mountain range that must never pop.

implementation_variants.name: Nanite-enabled HLOD output
implementation_variants.description: Both merge and simplify layer types expose 'Generate Nanite Enabled Mesh', letting the proxy itself be a Nanite mesh so that its own LOD is handled by the virtual geometry system.

hierarchical_lod.applicability_conditions: Any partitioned/streamed world with a visible horizon. Requires actors to be Static and to be assigned to an HLOD layer (via the actor's Details panel, a Data Layer default, or the World Settings default). Requires a build step (Build > Build HLODs or the WorldPartitionHLODsBuilder commandlet) that must run after any change to source meshes/materials/textures - Epic notes HLODs are not rebuilt unless their sources changed.
hierarchical_lod.limitations: The proxy is baked: any runtime change to the source geometry (destruction, season change, player-built structures) is invisible until a rebuild. Merged materials can artefact where source materials used world or actor position (Epic warns 'Merge Equivalent Materials... can cause artifacting... if world position or actor position is used to determine output color'). Merge Distance closes gaps, so windows and doors fill in, which is visible on buildings you can see up close. Proxies add their own texture and mesh memory, and 'Large geometry with small sampling has a very high memory cost' for the spatial sampling override. Build time over a large world is significant and needs CI.
hierarchical_lod.required_data_and_tools: An HLOD Layer asset per class of content; a proxy material; a deterministic bake in CI; a viewport mode to check the result (Level of Detail Coloration > Hierarchical LOD Coloration, plus wp.Runtime.ToggleDrawRuntimeHash2D at runtime); and, if used with Nanite, a Nanite-capable target platform.

impact.cpu: high positive - the whole point is collapsing many primitives into one, cutting render-thread primitive processing and draw submission
impact.gpu: medium positive - fewer draw calls and less vertex work; the proxy is usually fill-bound rather than geometry-bound at its on-screen size
impact.ram: low positive - unloaded cell actors are gone; proxies are small
impact.vram: medium negative - baked proxy textures and meshes are additional resident data
impact.disk: medium negative - proxy meshes and baked textures are additional content
impact.network: none

hierarchical_lod.quality_impact: Near-neutral if the transition distance is chosen so the proxy swaps at a screen size where the difference is imperceptible; badly visible if Merge Distance closes windows on buildings that are still recognisable, or if the baked material loses strong silhouettes.
hierarchical_lod.concept_impact: Allows the visible draw distance to be decoupled from the streaming range, which is what makes 'you can see the whole map' compatible with 'you only load a small part of it'.
hierarchical_lod.recommended_stage: production; it needs real content to bake and a working streaming setup to sit on, but it must be in place before open-world art is finalised so that silhouette decisions are made with the proxy in mind.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3d layer-type selection and asset setup + 3d merge/simplify settings tuning per content class + 4d CI bake pipeline (WorldPartitionHLODsBuilder with -SetupHLODs/-BuildHLODs) + 2d transition-distance tuning + 2d material artifacting fix-up; p80 adds a parent-layer cascade and per-biome layer splits

relations.note: HLOD exists to visualise unloaded World Partition cells; without partitioning there is nothing to proxy.
The Instancing layer type is explicitly described as ideal for imposter meshes, and has an 'Include Imposters' merge option.
Baked proxy atlas settings (target lightmap resolution, gutter size, texture binning) are the same parameter family as vegetation atlas packing.
If the whole world is Nanite, per-cluster LOD already provides sub-linear geometry scaling; HLOD then competes with rather than complements Nanite and may be unnecessary for opaque rigid geometry.
Epic notes 'Allow Distance Fields' can be disabled for HLOD proxies purely to save memory, which changes what the distance-field shadow/AO system can see at distance.

hierarchical_lod.verification: In the editor, use Level of Detail Coloration > Hierarchical LOD Coloration and fly the transition distance to confirm the swap is invisible; at runtime use wp.Runtime.ToggleDrawRuntimeHash2D. Then count draw calls with and without HLOD at the same camera position (wp.Runtime.HLOD 0 disables them), and measure the proxy's baked texture memory to check it against the VRAM budget.

gpu_compute_culling.problem: A CPU renderer that tests visibility per object pays O(objects) every frame in draw submission and per-object work, and on a console/low-core PC the CPU becomes the wall long before the GPU does. GPU-driven culling moves the visibility decision onto the GPU: the CPU submits 'draw the scene' once, and a compute pass expands instances into clusters, frustum/occlusion/backface-tests them against a depth hierarchy, and compacts the survivors into the argument buffer of an indirect draw. The point is not merely fewer draw calls - it is that the CPU cost stops scaling with scene complexity at all.

implementation_variants.name: Cluster-based culling with fixed-topology clusters (AC Unity / RedLynx)
implementation_variants.description: All meshes are split into fixed-topology clusters (64-vertex strips; 64 triangles per cluster) with precomputed bounds, culled by cluster bounds, and the surviving indices are compacted into an index buffer for MultiDrawIndexedInstancedIndirect. Pipeline: MULTI-DRAW -> INSTANCE CULLING -> CLUSTER CHUNK EXPANSION -> CLUSTER CULLING -> INDEX BUFFER COMPACTION.

implementation_variants.name: Two-phase occlusion culling against a generated depth pyramid
implementation_variants.description: Render the best occluders (300 in AC Unity) into full-res depth, downsample to 512x256, reproject last frame's depth, build a depth hierarchy, then cull. Phase 1 culls against last frame's pyramid and renders; phase 2 refreshes the pyramid and renders the false negatives. There is no separate low-poly proxy occlusion pass - occlusion is precise and WYSIWYG.

implementation_variants.name: Baked static backface culling per cluster
implementation_variants.description: Triangle visibility is precomputed for pixel frustums of a cluster-centred cubemap (6 bits per triangle, 64 bits per cluster fetched with one read) and looked up by camera direction; the pixel frustum is cut at distance, which permits false positives at oblique angles.

implementation_variants.name: Persistent-thread hierarchical culling (Nanite)
implementation_variants.description: Rather than one dispatch per hierarchy level with a global sync between each, Nanite uses a single dispatch with a persistent-threads work queue: dequeue a node, test, enqueue passing children. This avoids the 'wait for idle between every level' cost and the empty dispatches of the naive form.

implementation_variants.name: Cluster-hierarchy LOD culling (cut the DAG, don't traverse it)
implementation_variants.description: Culling and LOD selection are the same operation: a node is rendered when ParentError > threshold && ClusterError <= threshold, and culled when ParentError <= threshold. Forcing error monotonicity (parent view error >= child view error) guarantees a unique cut, so no DAG traversal or cross-thread communication is needed at runtime.

gpu_compute_culling.applicability_conditions: Scenes with very high object/instance counts and high depth complexity, where the CPU is the binding constraint. Requires an API with indirect dispatch/draw and (ideally) bindless or virtualised resources so that material/texture state does not force a CPU-side batch split. Requires accepting a one-frame latency in occlusion (both the AC Unity and Nanite designs cull against the previous frame's depth).
gpu_compute_culling.limitations: The AC Unity result is the honest headline: '20-40% triangles culled' but 'Only small overall gain: <10% of geometry rendering'. Culling triangles is not the same as being faster. The depth pyramid is from the previous frame, so fast camera motion creates overdraw and false negatives that phase 2 must repair. Two-phase occlusion means per-triangle occlusion culling is not done - a cluster containing one occluded triangle would have to be re-evaluated and re-rasterised, nullifying the saving. Divergence: one thread per triangle/meshlet means divergent formats and refill costs. Cluster granularity sets culling granularity: large triangles make large clusters, which makes culling coarse, so 'there are situations where drawing more triangles is actually faster'.
gpu_compute_culling.required_data_and_tools: A mesh preprocessing step that produces clusters (graph partitioning - Nanite uses METIS - with a max triangle count and shared-boundary minimisation), per-cluster bounds, a depth hierarchy generator, indirect-draw support, and GPU profiling that can see inside the compute passes.

impact.cpu: high positive - this is where the win is: AC Unity reported 1-2 orders of magnitude fewer draw calls and ~75% of the previous game's CPU cost with ~10x the objects
impact.gpu: low to medium negative - you spend real GPU time to save CPU time; the AC Unity torture test spent 0.28+0.09 ms on culling plus 1.60 ms on drawing, and the net geometry gain was under 10%
impact.ram: low - cluster bounds and hierarchy metadata are small relative to vertex data
impact.vram: low to medium - hierarchical metadata is always resident by design (Nanite keeps 'the full culling hierarchy always resident' because it is tiny)
impact.disk: low negative - cluster bounds/metadata are added to the mesh payload
impact.network: none

gpu_compute_culling.quality_impact: None in the steady state - culling is conservative by construction and one-frame-late occlusion is invisible except during very fast motion, where it shows as a one-frame pop of newly disoccluded geometry.
gpu_compute_culling.concept_impact: Removes draw-call and object-count budgets as a design constraint, which changes what level designers are allowed to build and what artists are allowed to place. It is the enabling technology behind virtual geometry and behind very large crowds/props.
gpu_compute_culling.recommended_stage: prototype for the pipeline shape (it determines how every mesh must be preprocessed), production for the tuning.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 15d cluster build/graph-partitioning pipeline + 12d indirect-draw renderer path + 12d depth pyramid and two-phase occlusion + 9d compaction and argument-buffer generation + 12d profiling and divergence tuning; p80 adds a full material/bindless rework and a meshlet-aware LOD system

relations.note: Nanite is GPU culling plus a cluster LOD DAG plus a software rasteriser; gpu_compute_culling is the shared foundation.
Two answers to the same question: runtime depth-pyramid culling vs offline PVS. Runtime scales to dynamic worlds; baked is cheaper but static-only.
Cluster culling is what lets an instanced-vegetation batch be culled at sub-instance granularity instead of culling the whole batch.
Cluster/meshlet locality only pays if the index order within each cluster is cache-optimal; the two are built in the same preprocessing pass.
Shadow cost in a GPU-driven pipeline scales with shadow pixels and lights per pixel, not scene complexity - so culling savings do not automatically translate to shadow passes.

gpu_compute_culling.verification: Instrument the compute passes directly and record, per frame: input instance/cluster count, survivors after each cull stage (frustum, occlusion, backface), compaction output size, and the ms of each pass. Compare GPU time with all culling stages forced to pass everything - the delta is the real saving, and per the AC Unity result you should expect it to be smaller than the culled-triangle percentage suggests. Repeat with fast camera rotation to measure the phase-2 / false-negative cost.

claims.statement: AC Unity's GPU-driven pipeline gave '1-2 Orders of magnitude less drawcalls' and ran at '~75% of previous AC' CPU cost 'with ~10x objects' (measured, SIGGRAPH 2015).
AC Unity culled '20-40% triangles (backface + cluster bounds)' in the main view, but the authors report 'Only small overall gain: <10% of geometry rendering'.
AC Unity culled '30-80% shadow triangles' - a substantially larger win than in the main view, which the authors attribute to the shadow-culling path.
AC Unity's occlusion depth generation on PS4: '300 best occluders (~600us)', downsample to 512x256 '(100us)', reprojection of last frame's depth '(50us)', depth hierarchy for GPU culling '(50us)'.

The RedLynx 'torture' unit test scene contained 250,000 separate moving objects, 1 GB of mesh data (10k+ meshes) and an 8k^2 texture cache atlas, and was drawn with 'Only two DrawInstancedIndirect calls' on a DirectX 11 code path.

In that 250k-object benchmark on Xbox One at 1080p: GPU object culling + LOD 0.28 ms, cluster culling 0.09 ms, G-buffer draw 1.60 ms, pyramid generation 0.06 ms, total 2.3 ms; CPU time 0.2 ms on a single Jaguar core.

Baked cluster-cubemap backface culling culled '10-30% triangles', using 6 bits per triangle / 64 bits per cluster, with possible false positives at oblique angles because the pixel frustum is cut at distance.
Nanite builds clusters of 128 triangles; the software rasteriser threadgroup size is 128 (one thread per vertex at the cluster level, 1 thread per triangle in the micropoly path).

baked_occlusion_culling.problem: Dynamic occlusion (hardware occlusion queries, or a GPU depth pyramid) costs render-thread time every frame and, on low-powered hardware, may not be available at all. If the world is static and the camera's reachable volume is known, the visibility answer can be computed once offline and stored: for each cell of space, the set of primitives visible from that cell. At runtime the query becomes a lookup. This trades rendering time for memory plus build time.

implementation_variants.name: Precomputed Visibility Volumes (Unreal / Lightmass)
implementation_variants.description: Visibility cells are generated during a lighting build above shadow-casting geometry; from each cell, actor visibility is stored. Tuning lives in [DevOptions.PrecomputedVisibility] in BaseLightmass.ini: PlayAreaHeight, MeshBoundsScale=1.2, MinMeshSamples=14, MaxMeshSamples=40, NumCellSamples=24, VisibilitySpreadingIterations=1, and bCompressVisibilityData=True.

implementation_variants.name: Sampling-aggressiveness tuning
implementation_variants.description: World Settings > Precomputed Visibility exposes Visibility Aggressiveness: Epic documents that 'More aggressive settings cull more Actors but cause more visibility errors to occur, like Actors popping in around corners', which is the direct quality/performance dial.

implementation_variants.name: Manual override volumes
implementation_variants.description: Precomputed Visibility Override Volumes let a designer force the visibility of specific actors/levels where the automatic result is wrong, and Epic advises placing them only in player-accessible areas.

implementation_variants.name: Portal/PVS-style baked sets (classic lineage)
implementation_variants.description: The same idea in its older form: cells and portals with a potentially-visible set per cell. Unreal's modern implementation is a sampling-based PVS baked by Lightmass rather than a hand-authored portal graph, but the trade (offline compute + memory for runtime lookup) is identical.

baked_occlusion_culling.applicability_conditions: Epic's own guidance is narrow and should be taken seriously: 'small to medium-sized worlds', 'typically for Mobile where dynamic occlusion culling is limited depending on hardware', 'mostly statically lit environments, restricted player movement, and somewhat 2D play areas'. It is the right answer when the camera's reachable volume is small and known; it is the wrong answer for an open world with a free-flight camera.
baked_occlusion_culling.limitations: Five hard limits are documented: it does not handle movable actors; it does not handle non-opaque materials (translucent or masked); cells are only placed above surfaces so 'Projects with flying modes won't get much benefit'; it 'does not handle streaming levels efficiently' because all data lives in the persistent level; and only static shadow-casting triangles occlude. It costs runtime memory and lighting build time. Larger PlayAreaHeight 'require[s] more runtime memory because more Actor visibility states must be stored'. Decompression itself costs frame time - stat initviews reports 'Decompress Occlusion'. And it is incompatible by design with a partitioned, streamed open world.
baked_occlusion_culling.required_data_and_tools: A completed lighting build (or the standalone 'Precompute Static Visibility' build step), hand-placed volumes covering only player-accessible areas, a tuned PlayAreaHeight, and the two verification stats (stat initviews, stat memory).

impact.vram: low
impact.disk: medium negative - baked data ships with the level
impact.network: none

baked_occlusion_culling.quality_impact: Neutral when correct; the failure mode is actors popping in around corners at higher aggressiveness, which is a very visible artefact.
baked_occlusion_culling.concept_impact: Raises the ceiling on how much static detail a small, dense, non-streamed level can hold on weak hardware. It does not help open worlds, and adopting it effectively forecloses streaming (see the streaming-level limitation).
baked_occlusion_culling.recommended_stage: production, once level layout is frozen - every layout change invalidates the bake.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2d enabling and first bake + 2d volume placement over all playable areas + 2d PlayAreaHeight/aggressiveness tuning + 2d override volumes for error spots; p80 adds long build times and iteration on popping artefacts across a large level

relations.note: Baked PVS vs runtime GPU depth-pyramid culling: the former is static-only and memory-bound, the latter is dynamic and GPU-bound. On PC-class hardware Epic's guidance is dynamic occlusion by default (SRC-WRS-016).

Documented: precomputed visibility 'Does not handle streaming levels efficiently. All data is stored in the persistent Level.' Baked PVS and a partitioned streamed world are effectively mutually exclusive.
For open worlds HLOD, not PVS, is the mechanism for reducing what is drawn at distance.
Nanite's two-phase HZB occlusion solves the same problem dynamically, including for moving objects; it supersedes baked PVS wherever Nanite is usable.

baked_occlusion_culling.verification: Run stat initviews and read 'Statically Occluded Primitives' (should be non-zero whenever the camera is inside a cell) and 'Decompress Occlusion' (the per-frame cost of this method); run stat memory and read 'Precomputed Visibility Memory' - in Game View or Standalone only, because Epic states the stat is not reliable in PIE. Then walk every playable surface at maximum camera height and look for popping at corners.

async_loading_pipeline.problem: Any world bigger than memory must load content while the game is running, and the naive version of that produces the two classic failures: a main-thread stall while a blocking load completes, and a spike of hundreds of small disk reads at the worst possible moment. Both show up as a hitch when the player crosses a cell boundary or opens a door. An async loading pipeline separates request (what is needed, by when), execution (background IO and decompression), and completion (a bounded amount of per-frame finalisation), so that no frame ever waits on the disk.

implementation_variants.name: Explicit soft-reference + request API (StreamableManager)
implementation_variants.description: Artists reference assets via FSoftObjectPath/TSoftObjectPtr so nothing is pulled in implicitly; code requests loads through FStreamableManager::RequestAsyncLoad with a completion delegate, and the manager keeps hard references until the delegate fires. Epic warns that hard UObject pointers mean 'you can end up loading 100% of your assets at game startup time', and that SynchronousLoad 'could potentially stall your main thread for too long'.

implementation_variants.name: Spatial/predictive prefetch driven by the streaming system
implementation_variants.description: Rather than explicit requests, the streaming system (World Partition cells, texture mips, Nanite pages) computes what will be needed from the camera and range, and issues requests with priorities. Nanite's version: a persistent culling shader outputs page requests with priority based on LOD error, the CPU reads them back asynchronously, adds missing DAG dependencies, issues IO for the highest-priority pages and evicts low-priority ones.

implementation_variants.name: Fixed-size-page streaming to avoid fragmentation
implementation_variants.description: Stream in fixed-size pages rather than variable-size objects, so that memory does not fragment and eviction is trivial. Nanite fills 128 KB pages at cluster granularity (~2 KB), achieving '~1KB average slack per page! (~1% slack for 128KB page)'; a root page is always resident so there is always something to draw.

implementation_variants.name: Batched small-read IO (DirectStorage-shaped)
implementation_variants.description: Restructure the request path so hundreds of small reads are submitted as a batch to a queue and completed on a fence, rather than issued as individual blocking file calls. This is the API shape DirectStorage is built for and is why it complements partitioning.

implementation_variants.name: Deferred install/GPU-side transcode on completion
implementation_variants.description: Move the post-IO work off the main thread: Nanite transcodes its disk format to its memory format on the GPU ('Currently runs at ~50GB/s with fairly unoptimized code on PS5'), and pages can reference data from parent pages without a CPU copy because 'the GPU has the context'.

async_loading_pipeline.applicability_conditions: Any streamed world, and any game whose asset set exceeds memory. The explicit-request variant is mandatory for UI/menu/inventory content where the need is event-driven, not spatial. The predictive variant is mandatory for world content. Both need a cancellation path: content requested for a cell the player left must be droppable.
async_loading_pipeline.limitations: Latency is irreducible: a request issued this frame is not resident next frame, so something must cover the gap (a lower LOD, an HLOD proxy, a loading screen, or gameplay that forbids fast travel). Asynchronous readback of GPU-generated requests (Nanite's design) adds a frame or more of latency by construction. Priority inversion is the common bug: a low-priority bulk request starves a high-priority one because the queue is FIFO. And the completion work (registering components, building render state, creating physics) is not free - it must be time-sliced per frame or the 'async' load still hitches.
async_loading_pipeline.required_data_and_tools: A request API and queue, priorities, cancellation, a budget for per-frame completion work, IO profiling that distinguishes queue time from read time from decode time, and a test that moves at maximum player speed along the worst path through the world.

impact.cpu: medium - you trade a large stall for continuous small background work; net CPU cost is usually slightly higher but the frame-time distribution is much better
impact.gpu: low to medium if transcode/install is GPU-side (Nanite's ~50 GB/s figure is GPU transcode throughput on PS5)
impact.ram: medium positive - resident set is bounded by policy rather than by accident; also needs a working-set headroom for in-flight buffers
impact.vram: medium - page pools must be allocated up-front and are not reusable by other systems
impact.disk: high - random read patterns increase sharply; this is the single biggest argument for NVMe-class storage requirements
impact.network: none (unless content is delivered over the network, in which case latency grows by orders of magnitude and the same pipeline needs a much larger prefetch window)

async_loading_pipeline.quality_impact: Positive - the alternative is visible hitching. The residual quality cost is that content may briefly appear at a lower LOD, which is exactly what the LOD/HLOD stack is for.
async_loading_pipeline.concept_impact: Determines whether seamless travel is possible at all, and sets the minimum spec (disk speed) in the hardware requirements.
async_loading_pipeline.recommended_stage: prototype; the request/completion architecture must exist before content exists, because content authoring rules (no hard references!) follow from it.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 8d request/soft-reference discipline across gameplay + 8d priority queue, cancellation and per-frame completion budget + 7d IO profiling and batching + 6d install/transcode path + 6d worst-case path testing; p80 adds a DirectStorage path, GPU transcode and a full content audit to remove hard references

relations.note: DirectStorage is the IO substrate that makes batched small reads cheap; the pipeline must be shaped to use it.
Partitioning decides what to load; the async pipeline decides how it is loaded without hitching.
VT is a specialised async pipeline with GPU-driven requests and a fixed physical page pool - the same architecture, applied to texels.
Nanite's streaming is an async pipeline with a fixed 128 KB page and a persistent culling shader generating requests.
Compression block size (Epic recommends 256 KB for Oodle) sets the minimum IO granularity that the loader can request.

async_loading_pipeline.verification: Record per-frame IO: number of requests, bytes, queue wait, read time, decode time, and completion/install time. Then run the worst-case traversal (fastest vehicle along the longest sightline) and assert no frame exceeds the budget. Separately, measure the p99 and max frame time, not the mean - async loading failures are tail events. Finally, kill the prefetch (force zero-lookahead) and confirm the game degrades to lower LODs rather than to a hitch.

claims.statement: Epic warns that with hard UObject pointer properties 'If you are not careful, you can end up loading 100% of your assets at game startup time' - which is why soft references exist.
Epic documents that FStreamableManager::SynchronousLoad 'may be fine for smaller objects, but it could potentially stall your main thread for too long'.
FStreamableManager 'keeps hard references to any assets it loads until the delegate is called' and releases them afterwards, so callers must hard-reference anything they want to keep.

Nanite streams fixed-size pages and fills them at cluster granularity (~2 KB) rather than group granularity, giving '~1KB average slack per page! (~1% slack for 128KB page)'; the root page is always resident so there is always something to render.
Nanite's GPU transcode of disk format to memory format 'Currently runs at ~50GB/s with fairly unoptimized code on PS5'.

Nanite's streaming is explicitly asynchronous and multi-frame: a persistent culling shader outputs page requests, 'Asynchronous CPU readback of requests' follows, then the CPU adds missing DAG dependencies, issues IO by priority, evicts low-priority pages and installs completed pages - so a request made this frame cannot be resident next frame.

terrain_clipmap.problem: Terrain is a heightfield far larger than any mesh you can upload, and it must have continuous LOD with no cracks, no popping, and bounded per-frame update cost when the viewer moves. Geometry clipmaps solve this by storing the terrain as a set of nested regular grids centred on the viewer: each level covers twice the extent at the same vertex count, so screen-space triangle density is roughly constant with distance and the whole structure is updated only in the thin L-shaped region the viewer has just uncovered. The GPU variant moves elevation into a vertex texture and does upsampling, residual decoding, normal-map generation and detail synthesis on the GPU, so per-frame update cost collapses.

implementation_variants.name: GPU-based geometry clipmaps (Asirvatham & Hoppe, GPU Gems 2)
implementation_variants.description: (x,y) live in constant read-only vertex/index buffers; z lives in a 1-channel float elevation texture sampled in the vertex shader. Levels are n x n with n = 2^k - 1 (default n=255, k=8, 256x256 texture); blocks are m x m with m = (n+1)/4 (m=64 for n=255); 16-bit indices cap m at 256 and therefore n at 1023. Each level is drawn as 12 blocks + 4 fix-up regions + an L-shaped interior trim; the finest level is a complete square.

implementation_variants.name: Toroidal update with upsample + residuals
implementation_variants.description: Clipmap windows use 2D wraparound addressing so only the newly exposed L-shaped (usually '+'-shaped) region is written each frame. Residuals (decompressed terrain data or synthesised Gaussian noise) are added to the upsampled coarser level using a four-point subdivision filter with weights (-1, 9, 9, -1)/16.

implementation_variants.name: View-dependent level activation by viewer height
implementation_variants.description: Levels whose grid extent is smaller than 2.5 x viewer height are deactivated, so the number of active levels L' <= L shrinks as the viewer climbs and the cost drops.

implementation_variants.name: Smooth transition band to hide level swaps
implementation_variants.description: Elevation is packed as zf_zd with a transition width w = n/10 blended linearly across the outer perimeter (alpha ramp 0..1), so moving between levels is continuous rather than a pop.

implementation_variants.name: Camera-following clipmaps for non-terrain volumes
implementation_variants.description: The same nested-grid-following-the-viewer structure reappears outside terrain: Nanite's virtual shadow maps use 'Nx clipmaps' for directional lights (16k x 16k, 128 x 128 pages), and Unreal's Global Distance Field is 'a low-resolution Distance Field... composited into a few volume textures centered around the camera, called clipmaps'.

terrain_clipmap.applicability_conditions: Heightfield terrain (or any data that is fundamentally a 2.5D field) on hardware with vertex texture fetch. Requires regular gridding - it explicitly gives up local adaptivity. Best when the terrain is broad and smooth and the camera stays reasonably near the surface (flying/high-altitude changes the active-level set, which the design handles explicitly).
terrain_clipmap.limitations: Regular grids cannot adapt: C-BDAM's authors contrast out-of-core chunked bintree methods, which are 'very efficient in approximating a planar or spherical terrain with the required accuracy' but need out-of-core management, against in-core nested regular grids which 'ignores local adaptivity' but compress well enough to fit entirely in memory. So clipmaps win on simplicity and memory, and lose where the terrain is highly variable in roughness. The classic implementation is planar-only (spherical needs the C-BDAM/P-BDAM family). Per-frame update is bounded but not free: the worst case (entire level updated at once) had decompression at 8 ms as the CPU bottleneck in the 2005 implementation. Triangles are ~5 pixels wide at n=255 in a 1024x768 window, which sets the LOD density.
terrain_clipmap.required_data_and_tools: A heightfield source, a compressor/decompressor for the residual stream (or a procedural synthesiser), vertex texture fetch, and a normal-map generator (or the elimination strategy in section 2.6.2).

impact.cpu: low to medium - drawing is a handful of DrawPrimitive calls per level (6*L+5 on average with frustum culling; 3*L+2 if each level is one instanced call), and the update was moved to the GPU (upsampling 3 ms -> 1.0 ms, normal-map 11 ms -> 0.6 ms in the source's worst-case table)
impact.gpu: low to medium - 60 million triangles/sec was the measured throughput in the source; vertex-texture fetch was measurably the bottleneck (185 fps without it vs 130 fps with it)
impact.ram: low - the compressed 20-billion-sample dataset occupied 355 MB of system memory at >100x compression
impact.vram: low - L elevation textures (256x256 float) plus normal maps at 2x (512x512 RGBA8)
impact.disk: depends entirely on the residual codec; the source's dataset was 355 MB compressed
impact.network: none unless streamed

terrain_clipmap.quality_impact: High and stable: constant screen-space triangle density, geomorph-free smooth transitions, and normal maps at 2x geometry resolution. The failure mode is over-smoothing in highly detailed areas because the grid cannot adapt.
terrain_clipmap.concept_impact: Makes continent-scale terrain with continuous LOD tractable on a single machine, and establishes the 'nested grids centred on the viewer' pattern that later reappears in shadow and distance-field clipmaps.
terrain_clipmap.recommended_stage: prototype; the data pipeline (compression, residuals, normals) is the expensive part and must be validated early.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 10d clipmap data structures and rendering + 8d toroidal update and residual path + 8d compression/residual codec or synthesiser + 6d normal maps and transition band + 8d profiling and level-count tuning; p80 adds a spherical variant or a switch to an adaptive scheme

relations.note: The residual stream is the compressed heightfield; compression rate decides whether the clipmap fits in memory or needs out-of-core management.
Nested regular grids (clipmaps) vs chunked bintree hierarchies (BDAM/chunked LOD): the former is simpler and fully in-core, the latter is adaptive but out-of-core. C-BDAM exists to get both.
Clipmaps bound the render/update cost; the generation budget bounds how fast new terrain data can be produced to feed them.
Clipmaps are centred on the viewer; an origin shift must re-centre them in the same frame or the terrain jumps.
Unreal's Global Distance Field is explicitly implemented as camera-centred clipmaps, and Nanite's directional VSMs use Nx clipmaps - same structure, different payload.

terrain_clipmap.verification: Count DrawPrimitive calls per frame (expect ~6*L+5 with frustum culling, ~71 at L=11), measure the update cost when the camera moves at maximum speed (worst case is a full-level update), and confirm there is no crack or pop at the transition band by flying across a level boundary at several altitudes. Check resident memory against the compressed size, not the raw heightfield size.

claims.statement: The canonical GPU geometry clipmap configuration is L=11 levels with n=255 samples per level (k=8), stored in a 256x256 single-channel float elevation texture, with block size m=64.

claims.statement: With view-frustum culling the GPU clipmap renderer averages 6*L+5 DrawPrimitive calls per frame (71 at L=11); instancing all blocks of a level into one call reduces this to 3*L+2 (35 at L=11); the finest level needs 5 additional calls.

The source measured 130 frames/sec and 60 million triangles/sec at L=11, n=255, 1024x768, with a transition to 185 fps when the vertex-texture lookup was removed - i.e. vertex fetch was the bottleneck. Final figures with terrain update during motion: ~87 fps decompressed, ~120 fps synthesised.

The demonstration terrain was a 216,000 x 93,600 height map at 30 m spacing and 1.0 m vertical resolution (~20.2 billion samples), compressed by more than 100x into 355 MB of system memory, on a 2.4 GHz Pentium 4 with 1 GB RAM and a GeForce 6800 GT.

Worst-case (full 255x255 level) update cost moved to the GPU: upsampling 3 ms -> 1.0 ms, normal-map computation 11 ms -> 0.6 ms, synthesis 3 ms -> ~0 ms; decompression stayed at 8 ms and remained the CPU bottleneck.
At n=255 in a 1024x768 window, clipmap triangles are approximately 5 pixels wide, which is the practical LOD density the scheme targets.

C-BDAM's authors characterise the nested-regular-grid (clipmap) family as one that 'ignores local adaptivity, but is able to exploit structure regularity to compress data so that it typically succeeds in fitting most if not all data structures entirely in core memory' - an explicit statement of the method's core trade-off.

Nanite's virtual shadow maps use 'Directional: Nx clipmaps' at 16k x 16k with a 128 x 128 page size and a 128 x 128 page table with mips - the same viewer-centred nested-grid structure applied to shadow depth.

virtual_texturing.problem: Unique, high-resolution surface detail over a large world does not fit in VRAM, and mip-based whole-texture streaming is a poor fit because it streams an entire texture when only a small part of one mip level is visible. Virtual texturing applies the virtual-memory idea to texels: a large (or huge) virtual texture address space, a small fixed physical page pool, a page table mapping one to the other, a feedback pass that determines which pages are actually visible this frame, and an on-demand loader that brings them in. The result is a memory footprint that is constant in the number and resolution of the textures and proportional to the screen's texel demand.

implementation_variants.name: Software virtual texturing (shader indirection)
implementation_variants.description: A pixel shader maps from the virtual large texture to the physical texture via an indirection (page table) texture. This is the design Sean Barrett published as Sparse Virtual Textures, explicitly 'mostly inspired by John Carmack's descriptions of MegaTexturing'. Barrett notes the key performance insight: 'packing the physical textures is crucial for performance' because sampling bandwidth/caching matters more than memory saved.

implementation_variants.name: Streaming Virtual Texturing (SVT) - pages cooked and loaded from disk
implementation_variants.description: Texel data is cooked and loaded from disk; suited to lightmaps and large artist-created textures, supports UDIM. Costs an extra indirection and has inherent latency before a requested page becomes resident. It replaces the conventional mip-based streaming model (whole mips, fixed pool) with page-granularity residency, which is the baseline it has to beat.

implementation_variants.name: Runtime Virtual Texturing (RVT) - pages generated on the GPU
implementation_variants.description: Texel data is produced by GPU rendering instead of disk IO, so complex layered Landscape materials, splines and decals are composited once and reused over hundreds of frames. This is Unreal's recommended use for Landscape.

implementation_variants.name: Hardware virtual texturing via tiled/reserved resources
implementation_variants.description: Use D3D11.2+ tiled resources (D3D12 reserved resources) so the page mapping is done by the GPU's page table rather than by shader indirection. Available on PC, but most shipped implementations remain software VT because reserved resources impose their own constraints.

implementation_variants.name: Virtual texturing as the enabler for a single-draw-call renderer
implementation_variants.description: RedLynx's reason for adopting VT was architectural rather than memory-driven: 'Key feature: All texture data is available at once, using just a single texture binding... No need to batch by textures!' Their cache was a virtual 256k^2 texel atlas with 128^2 texel pages and an 8k^2 physical page cache as a 5-slice texture array (BC5/BC3), giving 'Constant memory footprint, regardless of texture resolution and the number of assets'.

implementation_variants.name: Virtual deferred texturing
implementation_variants.description: Store UVs (and tangent frame) in the G-buffer instead of texels and resolve the texture fetch later in the lighting compute shader, so overdraw becomes cheap and the VT page-ID pass disappears entirely. 16+16 bit UVs into the 8k^2 atlas give '8 x 8 subpixel filtering precision'.

virtual_texturing.applicability_conditions: Large unique-textured surfaces (terrain, megatextured architecture), projects that need per-surface detail at high resolution without atlas baking, and renderers that want to stop batching by texture. It requires a feedback path (GPU -> CPU page requests) and therefore inherits multi-frame latency. It is most valuable when the alternative is a large number of high-resolution unique textures; it is least valuable when content is already heavily atlased and tiled.
virtual_texturing.limitations: Latency: a page requested this frame is not resident for several frames, producing visible low-resolution or missing texels if the camera moves fast or teleports. Bandwidth: page uploads compete with everything else on the bus, and thrashing on a too-small physical pool is worse than not virtualising (Unreal documents fixed pools per format group and their overflow behaviour). Filtering: aniso and trilinear need border texels or hardware support, which is why the id approach spends bytes on page borders. Software VT costs an extra indirection per sample; hardware VT (tiled resources) has its own constraints. Unreal additionally documents that virtual texture lightmaps have a lossy-compression option whose quality is 'lower... compared to regular color textures'.
virtual_texturing.required_data_and_tools: A feedback/render-target pass that outputs needed page IDs, a CPU readback and request queue, a fixed physical page pool per format group, a page table, a cook-time tiling/packing step for SVT, and profiling that can see page-fault counts and upload bandwidth.

impact.ram: low - page staging buffers

virtual_texturing.quality_impact: Positive when the pool is sized correctly (much higher effective texel density than a mip budget allows); the failure mode is visible low-res 'pop' or blur during fast motion or after a teleport.
virtual_texturing.concept_impact: Decouples texture resolution from memory, which is what makes megatexture-style unique surfacing viable, and (per RedLynx) can collapse the renderer's batch structure.
virtual_texturing.recommended_stage: prototype; like any streaming decision it constrains how content is authored and cooked.

relations.note: VT is an async pipeline specialised to texels: GPU requests, CPU fulfilment, fixed pool, priority eviction.

Nanite's author states geometry virtualisation is 'conceptually similar to virtual texturing' but harder, because geometry detail directly affects render cost and geometry is not trivially filterable.
SVT page reads are exactly the many-small-random-reads workload DirectStorage targets.
NTC attacks the same VRAM/disk pressure by shrinking the texels rather than by virtualising the address space; the two can compose (compressed pages in a VT cache).
Clipmaps handle terrain geometry; VT handles terrain surfacing - a shipped terrain needs both.

virtual_texturing.verification: Instrument page-fault count per frame, pool occupancy, and upload bandwidth; then teleport the camera and count frames until the image stabilises (that is the end-to-end latency). Sweep the physical pool size and find the knee where fault rate stops improving. Finally, confirm the filtering path: compare a VT sample against the equivalent non-VT sample at a grazing angle with anisotropy enabled.

claims.statement: RedLynx's virtual texturing setup: a virtual 256k^2 texel atlas with 128^2 texel pages backed by an 8k^2 texture page cache as a 5-slice texture array (Albedo, specular, roughness, normal, etc.) in BC5/BC3, giving 'Constant memory footprint, regardless of texture resolution and the number of assets'.

The stated architectural payoff of VT in RedLynx's renderer was not memory but batching: 'Key feature: All texture data is available at once, using just a single texture binding... No need to batch by textures!'

Barrett's stated lesson from the SVT work: the reason everyone likes DXT is sampling performance (bandwidth/caching) rather than memory saving, so 'the page table textures can be big bloated floats just fine... but packing the physical textures is crucial for performance'.

heightmap_compression.problem: A heightfield is the single largest asset in an open-world game and the one whose size grows quadratically with linear resolution: Ulrich's 16K x 16K Puget Sound dataset is 512 MB raw at 16 bits per sample, and a global dataset is tens of gigasamples. Raw storage is impossible on disk and impossible in memory, so terrain is never shipped raw - it is shipped as a compressed multiresolution representation that can be decompressed incrementally, at a known error bound, at streaming rates. The whole design space is a trade between how well the scheme adapts to local roughness and how well it compresses.

implementation_variants.name: Pyramidal / regular-grid compression (the clipmap family)
implementation_variants.description: Store the terrain as nested regular grids and compress those. Because the grid is regular, compression is excellent and the whole structure typically fits in core memory, which removes out-of-core management entirely - at the cost of ignoring local adaptivity. The GPU Gems 2 clipmap demo compressed a ~20.2-billion-sample dataset by >100x into 355 MB.

implementation_variants.name: Wavelet-based compression over a chunked bintree hierarchy (C-BDAM)
implementation_variants.description: Replace general triangulated patches with patches that all share the same regular triangulation connectivity and incrementally encode their vertex attributes when descending a bintree hierarchy, using a two-stage wavelet-based near-lossless scheme, with residual matrices stored per 'diamond'. Supports both mean-square and strict maximum-error metrics.

implementation_variants.name: Quantised 16-bit height with explicit Z scale (the engine-practical baseline)
implementation_variants.description: The cheapest scheme that works: store height as 16-bit fixed point over a fixed world range. Unreal's Landscape does exactly this - height values between -256 and 255.992 at 16-bit precision, multiplied by a Z scale (default 100, giving +/-256 m). Simple, exact in memory, and completely dependent on choosing the right scale per project.

implementation_variants.name: Residual/synthesis hybrid (compress the base, synthesise the detail)
implementation_variants.description: Store only a compressed coarse base and synthesise high-frequency detail from a small precomputed noise texture at update time. The GPU Gems 2 implementation offers both: decompressed residuals (~87 fps in motion) or synthesised Gaussian noise (~120 fps), plus a fully memory-free variant (L=9, ~59 fps).

implementation_variants.name: General-purpose LZ on top of byte-aligned, type-reordered data
implementation_variants.description: Nanite's lesson generalises: a compact in-memory representation is not automatically LZ-friendly. Pad to byte alignment, reorder data by type to minimise match offsets, and favour small byte values so entropy coding is effective - 'Increases raw size, but decreases compressed size'.

heightmap_compression.applicability_conditions: Any project shipping terrain larger than a few square kilometres at metre-scale resolution. Choice is driven by two questions: does the terrain have strongly varying local roughness (favour adaptive/bintree schemes) or is it broad and smooth (favour regular-grid/clipmap schemes); and is a strict maximum error bound required (favour wavelet schemes with max-error support) or is a mean-square bound acceptable?
heightmap_compression.limitations: Every scheme is a rate/distortion trade and none of them publish a universal ratio - the >100x and 0.25 bps figures come from specific datasets (a smooth US DEM and a global spherical dataset respectively) and will be much worse on rough, high-frequency terrain. Adaptive schemes require long preprocessing (Ulrich: 'a long preprocessing phase, and some size overhead for the disk file'). Chunked schemes store data in a form that is inconvenient for queries: Ulrich notes 'the data isn't in a convenient form for doing height/collision queries'. 16-bit quantisation with a fixed Z scale is a hard authoring constraint - pick it wrong and you get terracing.
heightmap_compression.required_data_and_tools: A heightfield source at known spacing and vertical resolution, an encoder with an explicit error metric and tolerance, a streaming decoder, and a quality check that measures actual error against the source (not PSNR against a proxy).

impact.cpu: medium - decompression is per update region; the GPU Gems 2 worst case had decompression at 8 ms on the CPU as the explicit bottleneck before it was moved to synthesis/GPU
impact.gpu: low to medium if decompression/synthesis runs on the GPU (synthesis was ~0 ms on GPU vs 3 ms on CPU in the source)
impact.ram: high positive - this is the entire point: 512 MB raw became ~214 MB at 4 m tolerance, and 355 MB for a 20-billion-sample dataset
impact.vram: low - only the resident clipmap/chunk levels
impact.disk: high positive - compressed size is the difference between shippable and not
impact.network: high positive if terrain is downloaded

heightmap_compression.quality_impact: Controlled and predictable if a max-error metric is used; visible terracing or lost features if a mean-square metric is used with a loose tolerance, or if 16-bit Z scale is misconfigured.
heightmap_compression.concept_impact: Sets the maximum terrain extent and resolution the project can ship, and - because terrain is usually the largest single asset - a large part of the build size budget.
heightmap_compression.recommended_stage: prototype; the codec choice is baked into the terrain data format and cannot be swapped late.

relations.note: Regular-grid compression is what lets a clipmap fit in core memory; the two are one design.
Compress-and-store vs generate-on-demand: the former costs disk and preprocessing, the latter costs runtime CPU/GPU and determinism.
Learned, per-material compression of texture sets is the same bet applied to texels rather than height samples; both trade encoder time and tooling risk for rate.
Terrain is usually the biggest single contributor to build size, so its codec choice dominates the distribution budget.

heightmap_compression.verification: Encode the source heightfield at several tolerances and plot compressed size against measured maximum error (not mean error) at the sample level. Then verify the streaming path: measure decode throughput in MB/s and confirm it exceeds the worst-case terrain consumption rate (travel speed x resolution x bytes per sample) with margin. Finally, compare rendered terrain against a raw reference at a fixed camera path and look specifically for terracing and lost ridgelines.

claims.statement: C-BDAM compresses a 29-gigasample sparse global Earth dataset to 0.25 bits per sample, decompressing and computing normals incrementally at run time for interactive full-screen flight with pixel-sized triangles.

claims.statement: The GPU Gems 2 clipmap demo compressed a ~20.2-billion-sample (216,000 x 93,600 at 30 m spacing) US terrain dataset by more than 100x into 355 MB of system memory.

On the 16K x 16K Puget Sound dataset (512 MB raw at 16 bits per sample), Ulrich's preprocessed chunk file was ~214 MB at a 4 m error tolerance and 'just over 1GB' at a 1 m tolerance - i.e. tolerance drives size super-linearly.

claims.statement: Unreal Landscape stores heightmap height as values between -256 and 255.992 at 16-bit precision, multiplied by a Z scale (default 100, giving +/-256 m).

In the GPU Gems 2 implementation, swapping decompressed residuals for GPU-synthesised noise raised the in-motion frame rate from ~87 fps to ~120 fps; the fully memory-free synthesis variant (L=9) ran at ~59 fps.

Ulrich lists as a downside of chunked storage that 'the data isn't in a convenient form for doing height/collision queries', which is a real cost for gameplay that needs CPU-side height sampling.
