virtual_geometry_clusters.problem: Artist-authored, film-resolution source meshes exceed every practical budget: triangle count, draw calls, memory and disk. Traditional LOD requires manual per-mesh LOD authoring and still pays linearly in instance and triangle count. Virtualised geometry (Nanite) solves all four at once by building a cluster hierarchy (in fact a DAG) over the source mesh, selecting a view-dependent cut of that hierarchy every frame at a target of roughly one pixel of error, culling clusters hierarchically on the GPU, rasterising the resulting pixel-sized triangles with a custom software rasteriser, and streaming only the pages of the hierarchy that the cut needs.

implementation_variants.name: Cluster hierarchy built by graph partitioning (METIS)
implementation_variants.description: Group triangles into 128-triangle clusters, then repeatedly group clusters, merge them, simplify and re-split into half as many clusters, producing a DAG (not a tree) because of the merge/split. Groups are chosen to minimise shared boundary edges (fewer locked edges) - exactly the graph partitioning problem, for which Nanite uses METIS.

implementation_variants.name: Crack-free LOD by alternating group boundaries
implementation_variants.description: Instead of permanently locking shared boundary edges (which 'collects dense cruft'), clusters in a group are forced to make the same LOD decision, and group boundaries alternate from level to level - 'What is a boundary in one level becomes the interior in the next level' - so locked edges cannot accumulate over many levels.

implementation_variants.name: View-dependent LOD cut with monotonic error and no geomorphing
implementation_variants.description: Forcing the error metric to be monotonic (parent view error >= child view error) guarantees a unique cut that can be computed in parallel without DAG traversal. Because the cut is chosen at sub-pixel error, 'If < 1 pixel error, then' no smooth transition (geomorph/crossfade) is needed - the pop is below one pixel.

implementation_variants.name: Software rasteriser for pixel-sized triangles, hardware for large ones
implementation_variants.description: Tiny triangles are terrible for a typical rasteriser (macro-tile binning, 4x4 micro-tiles, 2x2 quads). Nanite rasterises 128-triangle clusters in a compute shader with one threadgroup per cluster, choosing per cluster: 'Clusters with edges <32 pixels are SW rasterized'. Reported average: '3x faster!' than the fastest primitive-shader implementation.

implementation_variants.name: Deferred material evaluation through a visibility buffer
implementation_variants.description: Rasterisation writes Depth : VisibleClusterID : TriangleID; a full-screen quad per unique material then loads the vis buffer, derives barycentrics and interpolates attributes. This decouples visibility from material, eliminating shader switching during rasterisation, overdraw for material eval and the need for a depth prepass.

implementation_variants.name: Two compressed representations: memory (random-access) and disk (transcoded)
implementation_variants.description: Memory format is quantised, bit-packed and directly renderable (~17 bits/triangle, octahedral normals, implicit tangents at 0 bits). Disk format targets LZ: custom topology encoding at ~5 bits/tri, ~30% of vertices stored as references to parent pages, byte alignment and type reordering to help LZ, transcoded to the memory format on the GPU.

virtual_geometry_clusters.applicability_conditions: Requires DX12 SM6-class hardware (or current consoles) and, per Epic's doc, fast SSD storage. It is built for opaque rigid geometry - Nanite's own 'Future' slide states it does not yet support translucent or masked materials, or non-rigid deformation/skeletal animation, and is 'Not great with aggregates' (many tiny things forming a porous volume: grass, leaves, hair). It is an engine-architecture commitment, not a drop-in.
virtual_geometry_clusters.limitations: Masked/translucent materials and foliage/aggregates are explicitly out of scope in the 2021 design. Cost stops scaling at the DAG root: 'It ends at 1 root cluster of 128 triangles... At that point cost stops scaling with resolution' - which is why distant instances still need merging or impostors. Instance memory does not scale sub-linearly: '10M * float4x3 = 457MB', and Nanite has 'no special solution for merging'. Overdraw is real because there is no per-triangle culling and the HZB is from the previous frame. Disocclusion artefacts come from the two-pass design. And the build is a heavy offline graph-partitioning job.
virtual_geometry_clusters.required_data_and_tools: A mesh build pipeline with graph partitioning (METIS) and QEM simplification with attribute-aware quadrics; a GPU-driven renderer; a visibility-buffer material path; a paging/streaming system with fixed pages; and SSD-class storage.

impact.cpu: high positive - draw calls and per-object CPU work essentially stop scaling with scene complexity
impact.gpu: medium - you buy CPU freedom with GPU work: hierarchical culling, a software rasteriser, and a deferred material pass
impact.ram: medium - page pool plus the always-resident culling hierarchy metadata (described as tiny)
impact.vram: high positive per unit of detail - 882M Nanite triangles in a 7.67 GB memory format, versus 25.90 GB raw
impact.disk: high positive - 4.61 GB compressed disk format for that scene, i.e. 5.6 bytes per Nanite triangle / 11.4 bytes per input triangle
impact.network: none

virtual_geometry_clusters.quality_impact: Very high - the stated goal is 'no loss in quality' relative to the source art, with the LOD cut chosen below one pixel of error. The known quality gaps are the unsupported material/deformation classes and aggregates.
virtual_geometry_clusters.concept_impact: Removes polygon count, draw-call count and mesh memory as art constraints, which changes asset production (no manual LOD authoring, film assets used directly) and level construction (no modular-kit discipline needed for geometry reasons).
virtual_geometry_clusters.recommended_stage: preproduction to adopt (it dictates the renderer); production to tune.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 60d cluster build (graph partitioning + QEM + attribute metrics) + 50d GPU culling and LOD cut + 60d rasterisation (software path + HW/SW selection) + 40d visibility-buffer material path + 50d paging/streaming and compression; p80 adds multi-platform bring-up and a full content pipeline rewrite. Note: adopting an existing implementation (e.g. UE Nanite) reduces this to an integration effort of roughly 15-30d.

relations.note: Cluster hierarchy culling and two-phase HZB occlusion are the foundation Nanite is built on.
Both give you far-field geometry cheaply; Nanite's per-cluster LOD removes much of the need for baked HLOD proxies on rigid opaque geometry.
Nanite's own solution to tiny instances is 'Visibility buffer imposters' (12x12 directions, 40.5 KB per mesh, always resident) - impostors are the escape hatch when the DAG root is reached.
Nanite is 'Not great with aggregates' such as grass, leaves and hair, so foliage still needs an instancing/atlasing path rather than virtualised geometry.
Page streaming plus hardware LZ is the intended IO path; Nanite's own slide says hardware LZ is 'On its way to PC with DirectStorage'.

virtual_geometry_clusters.verification: Verify the LOD cut (freeze the camera, force a screen-space error visualisation, and confirm the error is below one pixel at all distances), the culling (count surviving clusters after each stage), the rasteriser split (log the SW/HW decision per cluster against the <32-pixel rule), and the streaming (fault count, resident pages, and whether the root page is always present). Then measure the two frame-time components separately: cull+LOD and rasterisation.

It also notes >90% of geometry is rigid, which is why focusing there first was correct.
Because the cut targets sub-pixel error, Nanite does not need geomorphing or cross-fading: 'If < 1 pixel error, th[en]' the binary parent/child choice does not visibly pop.
Epic's Nanite documentation restricts it to DX12 SM6-class desktop and current consoles and notes the streaming requirement; treat fast SSD storage as part of the platform requirement.

Do not size a project's disk budget from it without measuring your own meshes. The 3x software-rasteriser figure is relative to Epic's own primitive-shader baseline, not to a hardware rasteriser in general.

gpu_instancing_vegetation.problem: A forest is tens or hundreds of thousands of copies of a few dozen meshes. Submitting them individually is fatal on the CPU; even a single instanced batch per mesh type is wasteful because it culls at the granularity of the whole batch and cannot vary LOD or density per instance. GPU instancing for vegetation combines three things: per-instance data living in a GPU buffer, a hierarchical/cluster acceleration structure so culling and LOD happen per instance (or per cluster of instances) on the GPU, and indirect dispatch so the CPU submits nothing per frame.

implementation_variants.name: Flat instancing (ISM) - one batch, per-instance transforms
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's Instanced Static Mesh renders many copies of one mesh from a single component with per-instance transforms; it is the baseline and the correct answer for small counts.

implementation_variants.name: Hierarchical instancing (HISM) - cluster tree over instances
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's Hierarchical Instanced Static Mesh builds a cluster tree so that culling and LOD can be evaluated per cluster rather than for the whole component, which is what makes it viable at very large instance counts. This is also the structure behind foliage painting.

implementation_variants.name: GPU culled instancing inside a GPU-driven pipeline
implementation_variants.description: Instances live in a persistent GPU buffer, only sparsely updated; instance culling (frustum + occlusion) is a compute pass, and surviving instances expand into clusters which are culled again. AC Unity achieved '~10x instances compared to previous Assassin's Creed games' this way.

implementation_variants.name: Foliage-type authoring with density and cull-distance budgets
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's Foliage Mode paints Static Mesh Foliage or Actor Foliage with per-type density and cull distance settings, so instance population is an authored, budgeted quantity rather than an emergent one.

implementation_variants.name: Instancing HLOD for the far field
implementation_variants.description: Where instanced vegetation would still be too expensive at distance, Unreal's HLOD 'Instancing' layer replaces foliage with ISMs at the lowest LOD, on its own runtime grid and loading range - Epic states this type 'is ideal for imposter meshes, such as trees and foliage'.

gpu_instancing_vegetation.applicability_conditions: Any scene with high counts of a small number of repeated meshes: trees, grass, rocks, props, crowds. Requires that the instances are static or that per-instance transform updates can be batched into a GPU ring buffer. Requires that the cost of the vegetation's material (masked/alpha-tested, often two-sided) is understood - instancing solves submission and culling, not shading cost.
gpu_instancing_vegetation.limitations: Vegetation is usually masked material, which is precisely the class Nanite excludes ('Not great with aggregates... Grass, leaves, hair'), so virtualised geometry does not remove this problem. Enabling distance-field lighting for high-density foliage is off by default precisely because it breaks: 'some foliage assets (like grass) where you would have thousands or tens of thousands of instances would overflow the tile culling buffer', producing visible artefacts. Instance memory is the real scaling wall in a virtual-geometry world (10M instances x float4x3 = 457 MB). Overdraw from alpha-tested foliage is often a larger cost than geometry.
gpu_instancing_vegetation.required_data_and_tools: An instance buffer and cluster/hierarchy build, indirect drawing, a foliage authoring tool with density and cull-distance knobs, and profiling that separates cull time from draw time from shading/overdraw time.

impact.cpu: high positive - removes per-instance submission entirely
impact.gpu: medium - culling is cheap (AC Unity: object culling + LOD 0.28 ms, cluster culling 0.09 ms for 250k objects) but the surviving geometry and its masked material still cost
impact.ram: medium - instance transforms and hierarchy (10M x float4x3 = 457 MB is the cautionary number)
impact.vram: medium - same buffers plus foliage textures
impact.disk: low - one mesh referenced many times
impact.network: none

gpu_instancing_vegetation.quality_impact: Enables density that would otherwise be impossible; the quality risk is uniform-looking repetition (mitigated by variation/atlasing) and popping at cull-distance boundaries (mitigated by impostors/imposter HLOD).
gpu_instancing_vegetation.concept_impact: Turns 'how many trees can we have' from a technical limit into an art-direction choice, and makes biome-scale vegetation a level-design tool.
gpu_instancing_vegetation.recommended_stage: production; it needs the mesh set and the density targets to be known.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 6d instance buffer and indirect path + 5d hierarchical/cluster structure + 5d authoring tool integration and density budgets + 4d LOD/cull-distance tuning + 5d overdraw and material tuning; p80 adds a GPU culling pass and a custom wind/animation path

relations.note: Per-instance and per-cluster culling on the GPU is what makes large instance counts affordable.
Instancing reduces submission; atlasing/LOD reduces state changes and per-instance material cost. You need both.
Imposters are the terminal LOD for instanced foliage at distance; Unreal's instancing HLOD layer explicitly targets them.
Enabling 'Affect Distance Field Lighting' on dense foliage can overflow the tile culling buffer and cause artefacts, so it is off by default.
Nanite does not cover the aggregate/masked class that most vegetation falls into, so foliage needs its own instancing path even in a Nanite project.

gpu_instancing_vegetation.verification: Measure the three costs separately: cull pass time, draw/submit time, and shading/overdraw time (use a quad-overdraw or overdraw visualisation). Then sweep instance count and confirm the CPU cost is flat while the GPU cost grows sub-linearly. Finally, walk the cull-distance boundary for each foliage type and confirm there is no visible pop, and check the tile-culling-buffer artefact if distance-field lighting is enabled.

claims.statement: AC Unity shipped '~10x instances compared to previous Assassin's Creed games' after moving to GPU-driven rendering, and did it at '~75% of previous AC' CPU cost.
In RedLynx's 250,000-moving-object benchmark, GPU object culling + LOD cost 0.28 ms and cluster culling 0.09 ms (Xbox One, 1080p, DX11 path).
claims.formula: 0.28 ms (object culling + LOD, 1st phase) + 0.09 ms (cluster culling, 1st phase) = 0.37 ms
claims.context: Sum of two separately published figures for the first culling phase; the slide gives them on separate lines and does not publish the sum.

claims.statement: Epic documents that 'Affect Distance Field Lighting' is disabled by default for foliage because 'some foliage assets (like grass) where you would have thousands or tens of thousands of instances would overflow the tile culling buffer', producing 'unsightly artifacts'.

Even where rendering scales sub-linearly, instance memory does not: Nanite's slide gives '10M * float4x3 = 457MB' and states 'Nanite has no special solution for merging', with hierarchical instancing listed as future work.

Unreal's Hierarchical Instanced Static Mesh exists to add a cluster tree over instances so that culling and LOD are evaluated per cluster rather than for the whole component - the standard answer when an ISM's instance count grows.

claims.context: Page and setting categories confirmed via Epic's page; no specific default density or cull distance is asserted.

The instance-count and CPU-cost relationships also depend on how much of the crowd uses masked materials and skeletal animation, which the talk does not break out.

gpu_procedural_placement.problem: Hand-placing every rock, tree, grass patch and pebble across an open world is not affordable at modern world sizes, and painting them into textures does not scale to the density players see up close. Procedural placement generates the population at runtime from artist-authored rules - density fields, legality/slopemasks, exclusion zones, biome blending - evaluated around the player. Moving that evaluation to the GPU is what makes it fast enough to run continuously, every frame, as the player walks.

implementation_variants.name: Runtime GPU placement with artist-authored rule graphs (Horizon Zero Dawn)
implementation_variants.description: Guerrilla's shipped system 'dynamically creates the world of Horizon Zero Dawn around the player' and assembles 'fully-fledged environments while the player walks through them, complete with sounds, effects, wildlife and game-play elements'. The pipeline runs from a graph editor where artists define placement rules to GPU algorithms that build the dense world on the fly.

implementation_variants.name: CPU graph-based procedural generation (the engine-framework alternative)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's Procedural Content Generation framework is an authored graph evaluated on the CPU, with explicit static/dynamic generation modes and seeding/determinism controls. Deterministic, debuggable, inspectable in the editor - and bounded by CPU throughput, which is why it is usually baked at authoring time or run on a limited region.

implementation_variants.name: Density/legality fields evaluated in compute with scatter output
implementation_variants.description: The generic GPU shape: sample authored density and legality fields (slope, altitude, biome, exclusion) into a set of candidate points, filter, and write surviving transforms directly into the instance buffer consumed by the vegetation renderer - so no CPU ever sees an individual placement.

implementation_variants.name: Placement integrated with streaming (generate per cell, not globally)
implementation_variants.description: Placement is scoped to the streaming unit: a cell or chunk arriving generates its population, and the result is cached or re-derived deterministically from the cell key. This is what makes placement compatible with world_partition_streaming and chunked_procedural_terrain rather than fighting them.

gpu_procedural_placement.applicability_conditions: Large worlds with a small art team relative to world size, or worlds whose content must vary between playthroughs. Requires a deterministic seed/derivation (the same cell must produce the same population every time it is revisited, or the world will visibly change). Requires an authored rule layer that artists can control - the Guerrilla talk's emphasis on the graph editor is the point: procedural without artist control produces mush.
gpu_procedural_placement.limitations: The GPU-vs-CPU split is a real context difference, not a contradiction: Guerrilla's system runs continuously at runtime on GPU; Unreal's PCG framework is CPU-graph-based and is typically baked or bounded. Runtime placement consumes GPU time every frame in competition with rendering, and its result must be stable - camera-dependent placement that changes as the player moves is an immediately visible bug. It also interacts with everything downstream: gameplay volumes, navmesh, audio occlusion and save games all need to see the placed content. I have no verified numeric cost for any shipped implementation of this.
gpu_procedural_placement.required_data_and_tools: An authored rule/density authoring layer (fields painted in-editor or generated), a deterministic hash/random by cell, a compute scatter pass writing into instance buffers, and a debug view that shows density/legality/exclusion so artists can see why something did or did not spawn.

impact.cpu: high positive vs hand-authoring; low if the evaluation is on the GPU
impact.gpu: low to medium - continuous compute work that competes with rendering; no verified published figure
impact.ram: medium positive - no persistent per-object placement data; the rule fields are small
impact.vram: low to medium - density/legality field textures plus the instance buffers
impact.disk: high positive - rules and fields are tiny compared to baked placement data
impact.network: high positive for multiplayer - seeds replicate instead of object lists

gpu_procedural_placement.quality_impact: Can be higher than hand placement (density is consistent and biome-aware) or much worse (repetition, illegal placements, floating objects) depending entirely on rule quality. The risk is content that is statistically right and individually wrong.
gpu_procedural_placement.concept_impact: Decouples world size from authoring headcount, and makes runtime-varied or procedurally-modified worlds (desert -> swamp, as the Guerrilla talk demonstrates) a design tool.
gpu_procedural_placement.recommended_stage: preproduction for the rule layer (artists must author against it), production for tuning.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 10d rule/density field representation + 10d authoring editor + 10d GPU evaluation and scatter + 8d determinism and streaming-cell integration + 7d artist-facing debugging views; p80 adds gameplay/nav/audio integration and per-biome rule libraries

relations.note: Placement produces instance transforms; without instancing the output cannot be rendered.
Chunks give placement a natural scope and a deterministic key.
Placement scoped to streaming cells is what makes it affordable at open-world scale.
Slope/altitude legality masks derive from the same heightfield that drives the terrain LOD.
Both address the far field: HLOD bakes static proxies, runtime placement generates live content. Where placement runs continuously, HLOD proxies can go stale against it.

gpu_procedural_placement.verification: Determinism first: revisit the same cell many times from different approach directions and diff the resulting instance buffer - it must be byte-identical. Then measure the compute cost of the placement passes per frame and confirm it does not scale with camera speed. Finally, run an automated legality audit over the whole world (no floating instances, no instances inside geometry, no instances in exclusion volumes) and have artists review the failure list.

impostors_billboards.problem: At some distance an object covers too few pixels for its geometry to matter, but not so few that you can delete it. Impostors replace the geometry with a pre-rendered (or procedurally rendered) view-dependent image: a set of captures over the sphere of view directions, stored in an atlas, possibly with depth so parallax can be corrected. Done well, the object keeps its silhouette and shading for a tiny fixed cost and - critically - a fixed memory cost that does not scale with distance or instance count.

implementation_variants.name: Octahedral impostors
implementation_variants.description: Ryan Brucks' technique: view direction is octahedrally mapped to an atlas location, with dithered direction quantisation, an orthogonal capture projection with minimal extents fitted to the mesh AABB, depth+normal storage, and a short ray march to adjust parallax between directions (few steps needed because parallax is small).

implementation_variants.name: Visibility-buffer imposters (Nanite's tiny-instance solution)
implementation_variants.description: Nanite's answer to instances that reach the DAG root: '12 x 12 view directions in atlas', 'XY atlas location octahedral mapped to view direction', dithered direction quantisation, 12 x 12 pixels per direction, orthogonal projection fitted to the mesh AABB, '8:8 Depth, TriangleID', '40.5KB per mesh always resident', drawn directly from the instance culling pass and bypassing the visible-instances list.

implementation_variants.name: Billboard/silhouette-fin LOD termination for foliage
implementation_variants.description: The classic vegetation chain terminates in billboards; GPU Gems 3's SpeedTree chapter covers the representation side - silhouette fins extruded with a height map for detailed object silhouettes and relief mapping on the trunk - i.e. impostor-like techniques used even at mid LODs, not only at the end.

implementation_variants.name: Impostor-aware HLOD
implementation_variants.description: Unreal merges imposters into baked proxies: the HLOD 'Instancing' layer is described as 'ideal for imposter meshes', and mesh-merge layers expose an 'Include Imposters' option so existing imposter LODs survive the merge.

impostors_billboards.applicability_conditions: Objects that are viewed from all around, at distances where they occupy a small screen area, and whose silhouette matters more than their interior: trees, rocks, distant buildings, props, and - in Nanite's case - any mesh that has bottomed out at the DAG root. Requires knowing the view-direction set in advance (or generating it at build time) and a transition strategy into the impostor LOD.
impostors_billboards.limitations: The view-direction quantisation is the error source: too few directions and the object visibly snaps as the camera orbits. Parallax is only approximately corrected (Nanite notes 'Few steps needed due to small parallax', which is true only because the projection is orthographic and the extents are tight). Impostors are a fixed per-mesh memory cost whether or not the object is ever seen at impostor distance - Nanite's 40.5 KB per mesh is 'always resident' by design. They do not handle deformation, and Epic's own note on the technique is that they 'would like to replace with something better'.
impostors_billboards.required_data_and_tools: A capture pass (offline or at build time) producing the direction atlas with depth, a shader that maps view direction to atlas UV and does the parallax march, and a transition/LOD threshold per asset.

vegetation_atlas_lod.problem: Vegetation is the worst case for draw submission: many distinct species, each with its own material and textures, each needing several LODs, all instanced. If every species x LOD is its own material and texture set, you get a state-change explosion and a texture-memory blow-up. Atlasing (pack many species/parts into shared texture pages), combined with a properly constructed per-mesh LOD chain and shared materials, collapses that into a small number of bindings and a predictable memory and disk cost. This is the unglamorous half of making a forest run.

implementation_variants.name: Per-mesh LOD chain with screen-size thresholds
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's automatic LOD generation produces a chain of reduced meshes each with its own screen-size transition; this is the skeleton every vegetation asset needs before any atlasing or impostor work is meaningful.

implementation_variants.name: Atlas baking with gutters and texture binning
implementation_variants.description: When merging many source materials into one flat material, the critical parameters are gutter size ('Sets the space, in pixels, between UV islands at the original texture resolution for the baked material... Otherwise, artifacts can appear on the mesh as downsampling of the texture occurs at render') and 'Use Texture Binning' ('Calculates varying output texture sizes according to their importance in the final atlas texture').

implementation_variants.name: Leaf-card and fin representation with relief-mapped trunks
implementation_variants.description: GPU Gems 3's SpeedTree chapter is the canonical description of the representation itself: leaf cards, silhouette fins extruded and traced with a height map for a detailed silhouette, and relief mapping on the trunk - i.e. fewer triangles carrying more apparent detail, which is what makes the LOD chain cheap enough to be worth atlasing.

implementation_variants.name: Two-sided distance fields for canopy shading
implementation_variants.description: Where vegetation participates in distance-field lighting, Epic provides 'Two-Sided Distance Field Generation' because masked leaf/branch geometry 'cannot adequately be represented as a solid surface' - at the explicit cost that it 'will come at a higher ray marching cost'.

implementation_variants.name: Impostor termination of the chain
implementation_variants.description: The chain ends in an impostor (or a merged/HLOD proxy that includes imposters), so the atlas only has to carry detail down to the impostor transition distance, not to the horizon.

vegetation_atlas_lod.applicability_conditions: Any project with many distinct vegetation species instanced at scale. Requires a shared material model (otherwise atlasing is impossible) and a known screen-size budget per species. The atlas and LOD chain must be designed together: an atlas sized for LOD0 detail is wasted on LOD3.
vegetation_atlas_lod.limitations: Atlasing trades memory efficiency for authoring rigidity: changing one species can require re-baking the atlas. Gutters are mandatory and consume area - Epic's own warning is that without them 'artifacts can appear... as downsampling of the texture occurs at render'. Merging equivalent materials 'can cause artifacting in the merged mesh if world position or actor position is used to determine output color'. Two-sided distance fields for canopies 'come at a higher ray marching cost'. And masked materials remain expensive regardless of how well they are atlased.
vegetation_atlas_lod.required_data_and_tools: An atlas packer with gutter and binning controls, a shared vegetation material, an LOD generator with screen-size thresholds, and a memory report that attributes atlas bytes per species.

chunked_procedural_terrain.problem: Once terrain is generated rather than authored, and streamed rather than resident, it needs an atomic unit: something that can be generated deterministically from a key, meshed, LODed, collision-built, saved and discarded independently of its neighbours. That unit is the chunk. Chunked terrain is the decomposition of the world into fixed-size regions that are generated on demand, cached, and LODed as units - which is what makes infinite or near-infinite worlds possible, and it is the same decomposition that voxel/sandbox games use for storage.

implementation_variants.name: Chunked LOD (quadtree/bintree of preprocessed patches)
implementation_variants.description: Ulrich's scheme renders continuous LOD with geomorphs using batched primitives, is 'very friendly to texture LOD and paging data off disk', and its downsides are 'a long preprocessing phase, and some size overhead for the disk file'. Geomorphs smooth the transitions between chunk levels.

implementation_variants.name: Fixed-size generation/streaming/storage chunks (Minecraft model)
implementation_variants.description: Minecraft's chunk is a 16x384x16 block column that is the unit of generation, loading and terrain population, stored as 16x16x16 sections with palette-packed block states (4096 indices, min 4 bits), grouped 32x32 per region file (r.x.z.mca). One number cascade covers generation, streaming, saving and lighting.

implementation_variants.name: Continuous world generation with no pre-baked step
implementation_variants.description: No Man's Sky generates continuously as the player moves rather than streaming pre-generated chunks; the GDC talk is explicitly about 'the challenges Hello Games faced in developing a vast game-world as a small team'.

implementation_variants.name: Compressed batched adaptive chunks (C-BDAM / P-BDAM)
implementation_variants.description: For smooth spherical or planar terrain, chunks are bintree 'diamonds' of two right triangles sharing their longest edge, with shared regular triangulation connectivity and wavelet-coded residuals - giving both adaptivity and high compression, plus guaranteed overall geometric continuity.

implementation_variants.name: Chunk-scoped procedural placement
implementation_variants.description: Once chunks are the streaming unit they also become the natural scope for procedural content: a chunk key deterministically derives its population, which is how placement and generation stay consistent with each other.

chunked_procedural_terrain.applicability_conditions: Any generated or near-infinite world, any sandbox/voxel world, and any very large authored world that must stream. Requires that chunk boundaries be invisible - which means either matching LOD across boundaries, geomorphing, or skirts - and that generation be deterministic from the chunk key.
chunked_procedural_terrain.limitations: Chunk boundaries are the whole difficulty: cracks between mismatched LOD levels, popping when a chunk resolves, and duplicated work at edges. Preprocessing for chunked LOD is slow and its disk file carries overhead (Ulrich). Storage in chunk form is inconvenient for CPU gameplay queries - Ulrich: 'the data isn't in a convenient form for doing height/collision queries'. Generation is CPU work that competes with the frame, which is the central budget problem (see terrain_generation_streaming_budget).
chunked_procedural_terrain.required_data_and_tools: A chunk key and deterministic generator, a mesher, a LOD/crack policy (matching edges, geomorphs or skirts), a chunk cache with eviction, and a persistence format.

impact.cpu: medium to high - generation and meshing are CPU work unless moved to compute; this is the binding cost
impact.gpu: low to medium - uploading chunk meshes and LOD transitions
impact.ram: medium positive - only nearby chunks resident
impact.vram: medium - chunk meshes and their textures
impact.disk: high - save files grow with explored area; Minecraft's region format exists specifically to 'reduce disk usage by cutting down on the number of file handles'
impact.network: high positive - chunks are an ideal replication/download unit

chunked_procedural_terrain.quality_impact: Enables worlds that could not otherwise exist; the quality risks are all at boundaries and at generation latency (a chunk that appears late as flat or empty terrain).
chunked_procedural_terrain.concept_impact: Makes infinite worlds, player-modified worlds, and procedurally varied worlds possible; it also makes 'the world is a function of a seed' a shipping feature.
chunked_procedural_terrain.recommended_stage: prototype; everything downstream (streaming, saving, collision, placement, navmesh) depends on the chunk decomposition.

relations.note: Chunks define the unit; the budget defines how many can be produced per second. They must be designed together.
Chunked/hierarchical adaptive terrain vs viewer-centred nested regular grids: the former is adaptive and out-of-core, the latter is uniform and in-core.
Chunked storage is what makes it practical to compress and store only the chunks that were actually visited.
Chunk keys give procedural placement a deterministic scope.
Chunk keys must be in an absolute frame; an origin shift must not change them or chunks regenerate differently.

chunked_procedural_terrain.verification: Fly along chunk boundaries at every LOD transition and look for cracks and popping; then test determinism by generating the same chunk key many times from different orders and diffing the output; then measure generation and meshing time per chunk and check it against the budget implied by maximum travel speed.

terrain_generation_streaming_budget.problem: A streamed or generated world fails on a rate, not on a total. The binding constraint is not 'how big is the world' but 'how many cubic metres of world can be produced, meshed, uploaded and made collideable per second, versus how many cubic metres per second the player can cross'. If generation plus IO plus meshing is slower than travel, the player reaches the boundary of the finished world and sees flat, empty or popping terrain - and by the time that is visible in a build, chunk size, LOD policy and persistence format are already baked in. This method is the arithmetic that must be done before the architecture is fixed: derive the required production rate from maximum travel speed, then design chunk size, worker count and IO batching to beat it with headroom.

implementation_variants.name: Budget-first chunk sizing
implementation_variants.description: Derive the chunk size from the budget rather than picking a round number: required chunks per second = (maximum travel speed x streaming ring width) / chunk footprint; then chunk size is chosen so that generation + meshing cost per chunk leaves headroom at the target worker count. The clipmap work in GPU Gems 2 shows the same discipline for the uniform-grid case: update cost per frame was driven down from 3 ms to 1.0 ms precisely because the per-update cost was the constraint.

implementation_variants.name: Asynchronous generation with a distance-ordered priority queue
implementation_variants.description: Generate on worker threads with a queue ordered by distance (and by whether the chunk is in the view frustum), so the nearest chunk is always the next one finished. Unreal's async asset loading is the same shape at asset granularity: FStreamableManager::RequestAsyncLoad with soft references, so the work happens off the game thread and the result is bound when it arrives.

implementation_variants.name: Pre-baked generation at cook time vs generation at runtime
implementation_variants.description: Bake the world (or its height/collision data) offline and stream it, or generate it live. Ulrich's chunked LOD explicitly pays for the first option: it is 'very friendly to texture LOD and paging data off disk' but has 'a long preprocessing phase, and some size overhead for the disk file'. No Man's Sky takes the opposite path, generating continuously as the player moves, which removes the bake but makes generation a permanent runtime budget line.

implementation_variants.name: Two-resolution commit: cheap chunk now, refined chunk later
implementation_variants.description: Commit a low-detail chunk immediately so the world is never empty, then replace it with the full-detail version when the generator finishes. This converts a visible hole into a visible refinement, which is much cheaper to hide with a transition. I have no published measurement of this pattern; it is standard practice and is listed here as engineering judgement.

implementation_variants.name: Move the IO and decompression cost off the frame
implementation_variants.description: When the budget is IO-bound rather than CPU-bound, batch reads and decompress them outside the critical path. DirectStorage exists exactly for the traffic shape generated terrain produces: 'multiple gigabytes a second of small (for example, 64kb) data reads with minimal CPU overhead'. In the clipmap implementation the CPU-side decompression was itself the bottleneck at 8 ms, i.e. the IO and decode path - not the GPU - set the frame cost.

implementation_variants.name: Expose the cap as a settings tradeoff
implementation_variants.description: When the budget cannot be met, make the radius a user/quality setting instead of a hard-coded value. Minecraft separates simulation from rendering for exactly this reason: the documentation states that 'the simulation distance setting is ideally less than render distance because updating all entities within the simulation distance is more taxing on performance than the equivalent level of render distance', with Java Edition defaulting to 12 chunks (range 5-32 on high-performance singleplayer).

terrain_generation_streaming_budget.applicability_conditions: Any world that is generated at runtime, any world whose authored data is produced or converted on demand, and any streamed world whose streaming ring is smaller than the distance the player can cover during a load spike. Mandatory when travel speed is high (vehicles, flight) because the required rate scales with speed.
terrain_generation_streaming_budget.limitations: The budget is a product of terms you do not fully control: the player can always find the worst case (fastest vehicle, straightest line, most expensive chunk). Ulrich notes that chunked storage is also 'not in a convenient form for doing height/collision queries', so the generation budget is not the only cost - collision, navigation and population add to the same per-chunk figure. Pre-baking trades the runtime budget for a build-time cost and disk overhead. I could find no published end-to-end per-chunk generation budget for any shipped generated world, so any absolute number here must be measured on your own project.
terrain_generation_streaming_budget.required_data_and_tools: Maximum travel speed per locomotion mode, a per-chunk cost model (generate, mesh, collision, upload, save), a frame or worker budget, an IO throughput measurement on the minimum-spec storage device, and a stress path that crosses chunk boundaries at maximum speed.

terrain_generation_streaming_budget.concept_impact: Sets the real size and density ceiling of the world. A generation budget that is 2x too slow halves the playable world or halves its detail density, and that is a design constraint, not an engineering detail.
terrain_generation_streaming_budget.recommended_stage: prototype, before chunk size and persistence format are fixed; re-check at every locomotion change (a vehicle added late can invalidate the whole budget).

relations.note: The chunk decomposition sets the unit; this budget sets how many units per second must be produced. They are one design decision, made twice.
Generation is only off the frame if there is an async path with cancellation and priority; without it the budget is paid in hitches.
When the budget is IO-bound, the small-read throughput of the storage path is the ceiling, and DirectStorage exists for exactly that traffic shape.
Same rate arithmetic at different granularity: cells per second with a loading range, versus chunks per second with a streaming ring.
Compressed height data lowers the bytes-per-chunk term in the budget, which is the term that scales with storage speed.

terrain_generation_streaming_budget.verification: Instrument per-chunk cost (generate, mesh, collide, upload) and log the maximum sustained rate over a scripted worst-case run at maximum travel speed; then compare required rate = speed x ring width / chunk footprint against measured rate and demand at least 1.5x headroom. Verify on the minimum-spec storage device, not the developer's NVMe. Finally, deliberately starve the generator and confirm the failure mode is a graceful refinement rather than a hole or a wall.

claims.locator: Java Edition ticking paragraph: 'Using distance of 6 for instance, entities may move normally within a 13x13 chunk column around the player chunk...'

In the GPU Gems 2 geometry clipmap implementation, CPU-side decompression of the terrain elevation data was the bottleneck at 8 ms per update - i.e. the CPU/IO path, not the GPU, set the update cost.

claims.locator: Chapter 2 results (throughput figures for the clipmap renderer)
claims.context: Measured in 2004 on period hardware with a specific implementation. Useful as an existence proof for the rate, not as a budget for a modern project.

They say nothing about the correct streaming radius for a heightfield terrain, and no per-chunk cost or ms figure is published here. Source is a community wiki, not Mojang.

game_examples.fact: Generates continuously as the player moves rather than streaming pre-generated chunks, explicitly framed by the studio as a small-team strategy - i.e. the whole game is a live generation budget rather than a streaming budget.

distance_field_shadows.problem: Cascaded shadow maps get more expensive exactly where they get less useful: shadowing a large outdoor world with CSM means rendering more meshes and more triangles into more cascades, and the cost grows with shadow distance. Distance field shadows invert the scaling - the cost is per screen pixel rather than per shadow-map triangle - by tracing each shaded point through a signed distance field representation of the scene toward the light, and using the closest approach distance to approximate a cone trace for soft area shadows at roughly the cost of the ray trace.

implementation_variants.name: Per-object mesh distance fields plus a camera-following global distance field
implementation_variants.description: Each static mesh gets an offline-generated SDF volume texture; the global distance field composites per-object fields into a few camera-centred clipmaps, so only newly visible or modified areas need updating. Object fields are sampled near the shaded point, the global (lower-resolution) field further away.

implementation_variants.name: Hybrid: CSM near the camera, distance field shadows beyond it
implementation_variants.description: Epic's documented setup uses CSM for sharp shadowing near the camera and distance fields for the far region: 'When Distance Field Shadows are enabled, anything beyond the set value for Cascaded Shadow Map Distance will be shadowed using Distance Fields.' The worked example uses CSM to 1,000 cm and distance field shadows out to 1.2 km.

implementation_variants.name: Distance field ambient occlusion (cone-traced sky occlusion)
implementation_variants.description: The same representation gives sky occlusion: tracking the closest distance a ray passed an occluder lets 'a small number of cones compute a soft visibility for the entire hemisphere of a receiver point'. This is a separate feature from shadows, with lower fidelity sensitivity - shadow quality is more affected by field resolution than DFAO is.

implementation_variants.name: Two-sided distance fields for foliage
implementation_variants.description: Foliage represented by masked materials cannot be described as a solid surface, so a two-sided distance field generation option exists. The documented cost is explicit: it 'will work well for foliage but does come at a higher ray marching cost', and resulting shadows 'are never fully opaque'. It must also be opted into per foliage type via Affect Distance Field Lighting, because defaulting it on for grass-class assets overflows the tile culling buffer.

implementation_variants.name: Capsule shadows for skeletal meshes
implementation_variants.description: Distance fields only represent rigid meshes; for skinned characters Epic points to capsule shadows for indirect areas with DFAO and soft direct shadowing.

implementation_variants.name: Skip the feature and extend CSM / use virtual shadow maps instead
implementation_variants.description: On a project already built around virtualized geometry and virtual shadow maps, adding a parallel SDF representation doubles the asset build and the memory budget for shadowing. This is an engineering-judgement call, not a documented one.

distance_field_shadows.applicability_conditions: Large outdoor or large interior worlds with movable or time-of-day lighting where CSM distance is the limiting factor; scenes built from meshes of similar size; static rigid geometry (fields are generated offline). Requires feature level 5 (DX11+) on the target platforms.
distance_field_shadows.limitations: Generation is offline, so World Position Offset / displacement deformation causes self-shadowing artifacts because the field does not know about the deformation. Only static meshes, instanced static meshes, foliage and landscape (heightfield) are supported - no skeletal meshes. Non-uniform scaling is not handled correctly (mirroring is fine; scaling by 2x or less is 'not generally noticeable'). Shadows are computed at half resolution with a depth-aware upsample, so jagged edges can appear even with TAA. Larger Distance Field Shadow Distance 'reduce the culling efficiency', and a larger source angle on a directional light increases cost. All mesh distance field features are disabled on Intel cards because 'the HD 4000 hangs in the RHICreateTexture3D call to allocate the large atlas'.
distance_field_shadows.required_data_and_tools: Generate Mesh Distance Fields enabled in project settings, a build step (fields are generated offline), an atlas memory budget, per-asset Distance Field Resolution Scale tuning, and the Mesh Distance Fields / Global Distance Field viewport visualisations to inspect quality.

impact.cpu: low - tracing is GPU work; the cost is the offline build time
impact.gpu: medium positive to negative depending on configuration: the published comparison shows distance field shadows faster than CSM in every tested case (25-45% faster), but that is a 2013 GPU at 1080p
impact.ram: low - fields live in GPU-side volume textures
impact.vram: medium negative - per-mesh volume textures plus the global distance field clipmaps; a single mesh is capped at 8 MB (128x128x128)
impact.disk: medium negative - the generated fields are stored with the cooked assets
impact.network: none

distance_field_shadows.quality_impact: Gives soft area shadows with sharp contacts and no cascade seams over kilometre-scale distances, and avoids the leaking and over-biasing that shadow maps suffer in the distance. The quality risks are resolution-limited shadow shape (corners rounded off by the field resolution), half-resolution edge artifacts, and thin surfaces that cannot be represented inside the field.
distance_field_shadows.concept_impact: Decouples shadow distance from scene triangle count, which changes what distances are affordable and therefore what camera and world scales are designable. It also makes dynamic time-of-day practical at open-world scale.
distance_field_shadows.recommended_stage: vertical slice, once the lighting model is settled but before the asset library is finalised - the field resolution scale is a per-asset authoring decision that is expensive to retrofit.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3d enable and validate on target hardware (including the Intel disable decision) + 4d per-asset Distance Field Resolution Scale pass + 3d CSM/DFS distance split tuning per lighting scenario + 3d foliage two-sided policy and tile-culling-overflow QA + 2d memory/atlas budget; p80 adds DFAO, a full asset-library resolution audit and a fallback path for lower feature levels

relations.note: Instanced static meshes use instanced distance fields; the foliage tool's Affect Distance Field Lighting flag is what decides whether a foliage type participates, and getting it wrong overflows the tile culling buffer.
Both consume the same GPU time budget, and both are about reducing work at distance; their costs interact, so they must be profiled together rather than independently.
Fields are generated offline, so any world that streams actors in and out must ensure the streamed content has fields built and resident; a missing field is a missing shadow, not an error.
A virtualized-geometry pipeline already owns triangle-scale LOD and its own shadow approach; adding a second, offline-generated scene representation duplicates build time and memory.
Generated distance fields are cooked data: they add to install size and to the atlas memory budget in the same way compressed textures do.

distance_field_shadows.verification: Compare against CSM on your own scene and hardware: measure the shadow pass cost with distance field shadows off and on at the same shadow distance, at your target resolution, on the minimum-spec GPU. Then set the CSM/DFS split distance and sweep it. Inspect with the Mesh Distance Fields visualisation to confirm fields actually resolve the shapes you care about (a field that does not resolve the shape produces a plausible-looking wrong shadow). Confirm no Intel-card code path is reachable if that platform is in scope.

claims.locator: '### Quality' - 'The maximum size volume texture any single mesh can have is 8 megabytes with a resolution of 128x128x128.'

claims.statement: Same test setup: a directional light with 30k units of shadow distance and 6 cascaded shadow maps cost 4.9 ms with CSM versus 2.8 ms with distance field shadows - 43% faster, i.e. the advantage grows with shadow distance.
claims.context: 2013 hardware at 1080p.

claims.statement: Same test setup: one point light with a large radius cost 1.8 ms with cubemap shadow maps versus 1.3 ms with distance field shadows (30% faster); five point lights with a small radius cost 3.2 ms versus 1.8 ms (45% faster).
claims.context: 2013 hardware at 1080p.

claims.statement: Epic's documented hybrid setup sets the cascaded shadow map distance to 1,000 CM for sharp near-field shadowing and uses distance field shadows beyond that, shadowing objects up to 1.2 KM away.
claims.locator: '## Scene Representation' - 'the CSM shadow is set to 1,000 CM (centimeters)... RTDF shadowing is used, which shadows objects up to 1.2 KM (kilometers) away'

All mesh distance field features are disabled on Intel cards because 'the HD 4000 hangs in the RHICreateTexture3D call to allocate the large atlas'.

Two-Sided Distance Field Generation 'will work well for foliage but does come at a higher ray marching cost', and 'shadows from meshes with Two-Sided Distance Field Generation... will cost more as the resulting shadows are never fully opaque'. Affect Distance Field Lighting is off by default because foliage types with thousands of instances 'would overflow the tile culling buffer'.

game_examples.locator: '### Quality'
game_examples.non_transferable: This is an authoring-guidance anecdote from an engine doc, not a measurement: no resolution, memory figure or ms cost for Fortnite is published. It shows what kind of scene suits the technique, not what it costs in a shipped title.

neural_texture_compression.problem: Texture memory and texture disk size grow faster than the budgets that hold them: raising texture resolution by 2x costs 4x the texels, and block compression formats cannot follow because their rate is fixed per pixel. Neural texture compression attacks the rate itself - fit a small network per material over all of that material's textures and their mip chains, store the weights, and decompress on demand with random access - so that the same memory buys more texels and the same disk bytes buy more detail.

implementation_variants.name: Per-material network fitted at build time, decoded on demand at runtime
implementation_variants.description: The paper's structure: 'compressing multiple material textures and their mipmap chains together, and using a small neural network, that is optimized for each material, to decompress them', with 'on-demand, real-time decompression with random access similar to block texture compression on GPUs, enabling compression on disk and memory'.

implementation_variants.name: Transcode to a hardware block format at load, sample BC at runtime
implementation_variants.description: Use the neural representation only as the storage/transfer format and transcode into a conventional GPU block format once, so the per-sample shader cost stays that of a hardware format. This is the integration shape an SDK exposes; I have not measured it and no published cost is asserted here.

implementation_variants.name: Sample the neural representation directly in the shader
implementation_variants.description: Evaluate the network at sample time and skip the hardware format entirely. This is what 'random access ... similar to block texture compression on GPUs' enables, and it is what the on-demand decode path in the paper is for. Cost is not published in the material I could verify.

implementation_variants.name: Conventional baseline: block compression plus a general-purpose codec
implementation_variants.description: The comparison point for any NTC evaluation: hardware BC formats for sampling, plus a lossless-ish codec (Oodle Kraken/Mermaid/Selkie/Leviathan at a chosen effort level) for disk and patch size. NTC has to beat this on both axes - bytes and image quality - to be worth its integration risk.

implementation_variants.name: Selective adoption: hero materials and highest mip levels only
implementation_variants.description: Apply the technique where its rate advantage is largest and keep conventional formats everywhere else, limiting integration and training-time risk. Engineering judgement; no published guidance found.

neural_texture_compression.applicability_conditions: Projects whose binding constraint is texture memory or texture disk size, with a material model where many textures (albedo, normal, roughness, ...) are sampled together - the technique compresses a material's set jointly, so it presumes that structure. Requires a build-time fitting step and an SDK/runtime integration; the runtime decode must have random access, so it must fit the shader's sampling pattern.
neural_texture_compression.limitations: The technique is per material, so fitting cost scales with the number of distinct materials, and the paper's answer to that is a custom training implementation that 'surpasses that of general frameworks, like PyTorch, by an order of magnitude' - i.e. training throughput is a real engineering problem, not a given. It is new: as of the material I could verify it exists as a SIGGRAPH 2023 paper and an NVIDIA SDK, and I found no shipped title using it. I also found no published per-sample or per-frame decode cost, so its runtime cost is unknown from public sources and must be measured before adoption. Quality claims come with PSNR and FLIP metrics from the authors, not from an independent evaluation.
neural_texture_compression.required_data_and_tools: A per-material texture set with mip chains, a build-time fitting/training pipeline, the NVIDIA RTXNTC SDK (or an equivalent implementation) integrated into both the cooker and the runtime, and an A/B harness that measures image quality (PSNR/FLIP) and decode cost against your current BC baseline.

impact.cpu: unknown - no published runtime decode cost; a build-time training cost is certain and is described as significant enough to require a custom implementation
impact.gpu: unknown - depends on whether the representation is transcoded to a hardware format or sampled directly; neither cost is published in the material I verified
impact.ram: medium positive - the paper reports more texels for less memory in memory as well as on disk
impact.vram: high positive claimed - this is the primary benefit; 30% less memory than BC high while carrying 16x the texels
impact.disk: high positive claimed - the representation is compact enough to be the on-disk format
impact.network: medium positive - smaller downloads for the same visual density, if the format is used for shipping

neural_texture_compression.quality_impact: The claimed quality effect is resolution at the same memory: 4x higher resolution (16x texels) at 30% less memory than BC high, with quality the authors report as better than AVIF and JPEG XL. The risk is material-specific: a network fitted per material can fail on a specific material, and that failure is texture-level, not global.
neural_texture_compression.concept_impact: If it holds, it changes the texture budget equation - art direction can assume higher texel density than the memory budget would otherwise allow. It also adds a training step to the content pipeline, which is a new kind of build dependency for a game team.
neural_texture_compression.recommended_stage: evaluate, do not adopt: measure on a representative material set and on minimum-spec hardware before committing. Appropriate for a research spike during production, not for a shipping critical path in the near term.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 8d SDK integration in cooker and runtime + 7d build/fit pipeline for a representative material set + 5d quality A/B (PSNR/FLIP) against the BC baseline + 5d decode-cost measurement on minimum-spec hardware; p80 adds a direct-sampling shader path, per-material quality triage and a fallback path for materials the fit handles badly

relations.note: Both exist to decouple texel density from resident memory: VT decides which texels are resident, NTC decides how many bytes each texel costs. They compose rather than compete.
Texture bytes are usually the largest single term in both install size and patch size; a lower texture rate reduces both.
Same strategic move in a different domain: replace a fixed-rate representation with a fitted/compressed one and pay decode cost at runtime. Nanite ships; NTC does not yet.
If the format is sampled or transcoded on the GPU, it competes for the same decompression and bandwidth budget that DirectStorage is meant to saturate.

neural_texture_compression.verification: Do not adopt on the paper's numbers. Fit the representation on your own 20-50 most expensive materials, then measure three things on minimum-spec target hardware: bytes resident, decode/transcode cost per frame, and image quality (PSNR and FLIP) against your shipping BC baseline at equal memory. If the transcode path is used, measure the load-time cost too. Treat any per-material failure as a content bug with an owner, not as a tuning knob.

claims.statement: The project page teaser states: 'NTC provides a 4x higher resolution (16X texels) compared to BC high, despite using 30% less memory.'
claims.locator: Teaser caption (directly under the teaser image)
claims.context: Authors' own reported result on their own material set, from the summary teaser caption. PSNR and FLIP values are shown in the teaser image but I did not extract per-image numbers.

claims.statement: Same teaser caption: 30% less memory than BC high while providing the 16x texel count.

Combining the two published figures: memory per texel relative to BC high = 0.70 / 16 = 0.044, i.e. roughly 4.4% of BC high's per-texel cost, about a 23x reduction in bits per texel. This is derived from the teaser numbers, not stated in the paper.
claims.locator: Derived from the teaser caption figures
claims.context: Arithmetic on two summary figures; it assumes both refer to the same comparison and the same material set, which the teaser implies but does not prove.

claims.statement: The abstract states: 'We unlock two more levels of detail, i.e., 16X more texels, using low bitrate compression, with image quality that is better than advanced image compression techniques, such as AVIF and JPEG XL.'

The abstract states the method 'allows on-demand, real-time decompression with random access similar to block texture compression on GPUs, enabling compression on disk and memory' - i.e. random access, not whole-texture decode, which is what makes it usable as a texture format.
The stated key idea: 'compressing multiple material textures and their mipmap chains together, and using a small neural network, that is optimized for each material, to decompress them.'

The authors use 'a custom training implementation to achieve practical compression speeds, whose performance surpasses that of general frameworks, like PyTorch, by an order of magnitude' - an admission that training throughput is a practical problem, not an incidental detail.
I could not identify any shipped game that uses neural texture compression. The technique exists as a SIGGRAPH 2023 paper and as an NVIDIA SDK (RTXNTC); that is the limit of what I verified.

mesh_index_optimization.problem: The same triangles cost different amounts of GPU time depending on the order they are submitted in and the way their vertices and indices are stored. Post-transform vertex caches turn index order into shader invocations (ACMR ranges from 0.5 to 3 for identical geometry), triangle order turns into overdraw, vertex-buffer layout turns into memory traffic, and index data is compressible by roughly 6x. These are build-time transformations with no authoring cost: they change bytes and order, not the asset.

implementation_variants.name: Vertex cache optimisation (index reordering)
implementation_variants.description: Reorder triangles so consecutive triangles reuse recently transformed vertices. The metric is ACMR - 'average cache miss ratio, which is the ratio of the total number of vertex invocations to the triangle count. The worst-case ACMR is 3... on regular grids the optimal ACMR approaches 0.5. On real meshes it usually is in [0.5..1.5] range'. Historically GPUs used 'a small fixed-size post-transform cache (16-32 vertices)'.

implementation_variants.name: Overdraw optimisation (triangle reordering)
implementation_variants.description: Reorder triangles front-to-back to reduce pixel shader invocations, with a threshold parameter: '1.05 meaning that the resulting ratio should be at most 5% worse than before the optimization' for the vertex cache. Overdraw's best case 'is 1.0 - each pixel is shaded once'.

implementation_variants.name: Vertex fetch optimisation (vertex buffer reordering)
implementation_variants.description: Reorder vertices so they are read in memory order as well as in index order; the metric is overfetch, 'the ratio between the number of bytes read from the vertex buffer to the total number of bytes in the vertex buffer... the best case is 1.0'.

implementation_variants.name: Index and vertex buffer encoding
implementation_variants.description: Compress the buffers themselves: 'the index codec targets 1 byte per triangle as a best case (6x smaller than raw 16-bit index data); on real-world meshes, it's typical to achieve 1-1.2 bytes per triangle', with decoders running '3-6 GB/s on modern desktop CPUs'. Vertex data typically compresses 'around 2-4x (compared to already quantized and optimally packed data)'.

implementation_variants.name: Meshlet / cluster generation for mesh-shader and cluster-culling pipelines
implementation_variants.description: Split meshes into meshlets that maximise internal vertex reuse while minimising radius and direction divergence, which is the unit both GPU culling and virtualised geometry operate on. The meshlet codec targets '5-7 bits per triangle for triangle data', and '9-12 bits per triangle in aggregate' with vertex references. Hardware limits differ: 'for NVidia the values of 64 and 126 are recommended' for max_vertices/max_triangles, with 64/96 as a more realistic alternative and '64 and 64, or 128 and 128' for earlier AMD GPUs.

implementation_variants.name: Engine-integrated automatic LOD generation and simplification
implementation_variants.description: The same library primitives power automatic LOD reduction in-engine; the simplifier's target error is relative - '1e-2f means that simplifier will try to maintain the error to be below 1% of the mesh extents'. Unreal exposes automatic static mesh LOD generation with its own reduction settings.

mesh_index_optimization.applicability_conditions: Any project that ships triangles and controls its cook pipeline. Free to adopt when it is a build step over existing assets; requires pipeline work when the runtime must decode the buffers (encoding is only worth it if the decoder runs on the load path). Mandatory if you are building a meshlet/cluster pipeline, since cluster topology quality decides culling efficiency.
mesh_index_optimization.limitations: These optimisations change ordering and bytes, not geometry - they cannot fix a mesh that is simply too dense. Several are in tension: overdraw optimisation explicitly trades vertex cache efficiency (the 1.05 threshold parameter), and triangle strips buy smaller index buffers at the cost of '~5% worse ACMR'. Encoding is only a win if decode time on the load path is cheaper than the IO it saves, which depends on storage speed. Cluster/meshlet sizing is hardware-specific and the recommended values differ between vendors.
mesh_index_optimization.required_data_and_tools: A cook/build step with access to the raw index and vertex buffers, the library or an equivalent implementation, an analyser pass (ACMR, ATVR, overdraw, overfetch) to prove the change, and - if encoding is used - a decoder on the load path plus a measurement of decode throughput on minimum-spec hardware.

impact.cpu: low negative at load if buffers are encoded (3-6 GB/s decode on modern desktop CPUs), otherwise negligible
impact.gpu: medium positive - fewer vertex shader invocations (ACMR 0.5-1.5 vs worst-case 3), less overdraw and less vertex fetch traffic
impact.ram: low positive - encoded buffers are smaller in memory if kept encoded
impact.vram: medium positive - index data at ~1 byte/triangle instead of 6, and vertex data 2-4x smaller; also fewer bytes fetched per frame
impact.disk: medium positive - roughly a 6x reduction on index data and 2-4x on vertex data
impact.network: medium positive - same reduction applies to downloaded content

mesh_index_optimization.quality_impact: None for the reordering and encoding variants - output geometry is identical (or within a quantisation error you choose). Quality risk appears only when the simplifier is involved: LOD reduction is lossy and its error is expressed in percent of mesh extents.
mesh_index_optimization.concept_impact: Low concept impact, high practical impact: it is one of the few optimisations that buys frame time and disk space with no art-direction cost and no authoring change. It is also a prerequisite for cluster-based rendering rather than an alternative to it.
mesh_index_optimization.recommended_stage: production, as a cook-pipeline step - adopt early enough that the analyser numbers can gate content (a mesh with ACMR above a threshold is a content bug).

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2d integrate the library into the cook step + 2d analyser pass and CI thresholds + 2d vertex/index encoding and decoder on the load path + 2d measure on minimum-spec hardware; p80 adds meshlet generation tuned per vendor, simplification/LOD policy and a decode-vs-IO tradeoff study

relations.note: Meshlet generation is the shared primitive: both cluster culling and virtualised geometry need clusters that maximise internal vertex reuse and minimise radius.
Cluster culling operates on the meshlets this step produces; cluster topology directly determines how much the culler can reject.
The simplifier and its relative-error metric are what generate the LOD chain that HLOD and automatic LOD systems consume.
Encoded buffers reduce both install size and the number of bytes the loader must read; whether that also reduces load time depends on the decode-vs-IO tradeoff.
On very fast storage, decoding compressed buffers on the CPU can cost more than the IO it saves; the tradeoff must be measured against the actual storage path.

mesh_index_optimization.verification: Run the analysers on the current asset set before and after: ACMR (target the low end of 0.5-1.5), ATVR, overdraw and overfetch. Confirm the shipped index data is in the 1-1.2 bytes/triangle range if encoded, and measure decode time on the minimum-spec CPU against the IO time saved. For meshlets, verify the chosen max_vertices/max_triangles against the actual target GPUs and measure culling effectiveness, not just cluster statistics.

build_size_startup_budgets.problem: Install size, patch size and startup time are three different budgets that the same packaging decision spends. A pack file that is one 25 GB blob downloads as one 25 GB blob, patches badly, and holds a hard reference chain that loads at startup whether or not the player needs it. Treating 'how big is the build' as a single number hides all three; treating them as separate budgets with separate mechanisms - compression method and level, chunk granularity, reference discipline at startup - is what keeps a large world shippable on a store with a patch pipeline.

implementation_variants.name: Compressed pack / IOStore files with an explicitly chosen codec and level
implementation_variants.description: Enable compression on the cooked packages and choose method and effort deliberately. Oodle Data exposes four methods (Kraken high compression with good decode speed and 'the usual default'; Mermaid less compression and faster decode; Selkie even less and faster; Leviathan more compression and slower to decode) and a compression level 'between -4 and 9' that trades encode time only - 'The decoder at runtime never needs to know what method was used.' Unreal's own defaults differ per configuration: 3 for Debug/Development, 5 for Test/Shipping, 7 for Distribution.

implementation_variants.name: Compression block size matched to the patch system
implementation_variants.description: Compression block size is a patch-size parameter, not just a ratio parameter: Epic recommends '-compressionblocksize=256KB' for Oodle, and Valve's guidance is to align Unreal pack-file padding to the SteamPipe chunk size ('-patchpaddingalign=1048576 -blocksize=1048576', up from the 2048 default) so that re-alignments shift assets by a multiple of the delta block size.

implementation_variants.name: Chunking by primary asset label / by world partition cell
implementation_variants.description: Decide what is in which downloadable unit: chunking via primary asset labels or, in a World Partition world, via its own chunking, so that a patch touching one region does not invalidate another region's bytes. This is the mechanism that turns 'we changed a level' into 'the player downloads a small delta'.

implementation_variants.name: Startup reference discipline
implementation_variants.description: Anything hard-referenced by a startup-loaded asset is loaded at startup. Unreal's async loading documentation makes the alternative explicit: soft references (FSoftObjectPath / TSoftObjectPtr) plus FStreamableManager::RequestAsyncLoad, so the reference exists without the load. Hard-reference chains are the usual cause of a startup spike that no amount of compression fixes.

implementation_variants.name: Limited pack-file size and limited scope per pack
implementation_variants.description: Valve's guidance is direct: 'limit the size of pack files. Probably one or two gigabytes (GB) is sufficiently large - more than enough to allow efficient disk reads when loading the game', and 'keep the scope of assets within a single pack file fairly limited. Perhaps to a single game level, or unlockable feature.' The reason is patch cost, not read performance.

implementation_variants.name: CI size gates
implementation_variants.description: Track install size, largest asset and startup loaded-set size as build artefacts with thresholds, so a regression is caught by the person who caused it. This is engineering judgement; no published guidance from my sources.

build_size_startup_budgets.applicability_conditions: Any shipped project with an install footprint large enough that download or disk space is a purchase barrier, any project with a patch pipeline, and any project where startup time is a review or platform-certification concern. The smaller the team, the more this should be policy rather than measurement - the decisions are cheap and the mistakes are expensive.
build_size_startup_budgets.limitations: Compression level buys bytes with build time, and the highest levels (up to 9) are only worth it for distribution builds; method choice trades decode speed, which is a runtime cost on the load path. Chunking adds process: someone must own chunk assignment, and a wrong assignment is invisible until a patch is unexpectedly huge. Aggressive startup trimming moves cost to first-use hitches rather than eliminating it. I found no published install-size or startup-time budget from a specific shipped title in the sources I could verify, so absolute targets must come from your own platform holders and your own market.
build_size_startup_budgets.required_data_and_tools: A packaging configuration you can vary (method, level, block size, chunk assignment), a patch-size measurement against the previous build, a startup load trace, and a size dashboard that records install size and largest assets per build.

impact.cpu: medium negative at build time (higher compression levels) and low at runtime (decode), depending on method
impact.gpu: none
impact.ram: low positive - a smaller startup loaded set means less resident memory at boot
impact.vram: none directly
impact.disk: high positive - compression and chunking are the two levers on install size and on how much of it a patch replaces
impact.network: high positive - patch size is what players actually experience; distributed TOC and alignment mistakes can make a small change download 'over half the entire file'

build_size_startup_budgets.quality_impact: Indirect but real: install size affects conversion, and startup time affects first-impression reviews. Neither is a rendering quality issue; both are product quality issues with engineering causes.
build_size_startup_budgets.concept_impact: Constrains what content can ship. A 100 GB install is a different product from a 40 GB install regardless of what is in it, and if the patch pipeline is bad, live-service content cadence is limited by download size rather than by production capacity.
build_size_startup_budgets.recommended_stage: production setup, early - the pack/chunk layout must be right before the first external build, because changing it later invalidates every existing patch.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2d compression method/level sweep on target platforms + 3d chunk assignment policy and primary asset labels + 3d patch-size measurement against the previous build + 2d startup reference audit and soft-reference conversion; p80 adds per-platform hardware-compression overrides, a size dashboard in CI and a pack-layout migration

relations.note: Pack layout is the single biggest determinant of patch size; the two are one decision viewed from the developer side and the player side.
Soft references plus async loading is how a startup budget is actually enforced; compression cannot fix a hard-reference chain.
Compressed packages only reach the CPU fast if the IO path can saturate the device; DirectStorage is the Windows mechanism for that.
Textures are usually the largest single term in install size, so a lower texture rate attacks the same budget from the content side.
A world partitioned into many cells must have a chunk assignment that keeps the streaming unit and the downloadable unit aligned, or streaming and patching fight each other.

build_size_startup_budgets.verification: Measure three numbers per build, on the actual store pipeline: compressed install size, patch size against the previous live build for a representative small change, and cold-start time to interactive on the minimum-spec storage device. Then run the experiment that catches the common failure - change one small asset, rebuild, and confirm the patch is small. If it is not, the pack layout is wrong, not the compression.
