differential_patch_pipeline.problem: A live game ships the same bytes over and over. If the packaging does not let the patch system recognise what is unchanged, a ten-byte content change becomes a multi-gigabyte download and a multi-gigabyte local rebuild on the player's disk - and the cost is paid by the player, on the worst hardware in the install base, every single update. Differential patching is the set of packaging and pipeline decisions that make 'what changed' recognisable to the delivery system: chunk granularity, byte stability, and a manifest.

implementation_variants.name: Fixed-size chunk deduplication against the previous build
implementation_variants.description: Split every file into fixed-size chunks and reuse the ones that match the previous build. SteamPipe: 'Each file is scanned and divided into small chunks of about 1MB. If the depot has been built before, this partitioning will preserve as many of the unchanged chunks as possible' - then only new chunks are compressed, encrypted and uploaded. Updates use the same path as the initial build - 'To update your game or software build, simply follow the same instructions for creating your initial builds in SteamPipe' - and customers receive the build marked as the Default build.

implementation_variants.name: Engine-side layout alignment matched to the platform chunk size
implementation_variants.description: Make the pack file's internal block boundaries a multiple of the platform's delta block size so a content change only dirties its own blocks. For Unreal on Steam this is the documented '-patchpaddingalign=1048576 -blocksize=1048576' change; without it, 'this alignment can cause cascading asset shifts when building new versions, especially if pack file compression is enabled'.

implementation_variants.name: Whole-file binary delta
implementation_variants.description: Compute a binary delta between old and new versions of a file rather than matching chunks. SteamPipe describes itself this way - 'an efficient patching algorithm based on binary deltas, only changing the modified portions of existing content files' - and it is the right approach for large monolithic files that cannot be re-laid out.

implementation_variants.name: Per-level / per-feature chunk assignment
implementation_variants.description: Assign assets to downloadable units by level or feature so an update touches one unit. Unreal exposes chunking through chunk IDs and primary asset labels, and World Partition has its own chunking path; Valve's advice is the same: 'keep the scope of assets within a single pack file fairly limited. Perhaps to a single game level, or unlockable feature.'

implementation_variants.name: Manifest-based versioning with preload deltas
implementation_variants.description: Identify each build by a manifest and deliver preloads as deltas from the previous build: 'each manifest is identified by a unique 64-bit manifest ID', and 'Preload updates are delivered as a delta patch from the previous build in the same way they are after release' - with the caveat that preloads are stored on disk until release, so 'multiple large updates can end up consuming a large amount of space on-disk'.

implementation_variants.name: Do not reorder assets for load-time optimisation without measuring the patch cost
implementation_variants.description: The documented trap: 'if, in the process of creating an update for your game, you wish to optimize load times by reordering assets within the pack file, be cognizant of the fact that it may result in a very large download for that update. We recommend only doing this if the performance improvements are significant.'

differential_patch_pipeline.applicability_conditions: Any game that ships more than one build to the same players - which is every live game and every game with a day-one patch. Critical on platforms where the patch system is fixed and outside your control (Steam), because there you can only adapt your packaging to it, not the reverse.
differential_patch_pipeline.limitations: The mechanism only works if the bytes are stable. Valve's worst case is explicit: with a distributed TOC using absolute byte offsets, 'even changing a few small assets in a pack file results in clients needing to download over half the entire file to update'. Sub-megabyte asset shuffling defeats chunk matching entirely because 'the previously determined 1-MB chunks will no longer be present within the file'. Compression or encryption that crosses asset boundaries 'will spread out changes and require clients to download more data than necessary'. And the local rebuild cost is independent of the download size: a 25 GB pack file is rebuilt in full even for a 10-byte change.
differential_patch_pipeline.required_data_and_tools: A pack/build layout whose block size matches the platform delta size, a way to measure actual patch size before release (Valve: 'Ability to see the update size of a build before setting it live'), a binary diff tool to verify that the changed bytes match the changed assets, and a per-chunk content ownership map.

impact.gpu: none
impact.ram: none
impact.vram: none
impact.disk: high - local rebuild cost is driven by pack size, not by change size; preload deltas also consume disk until release

differential_patch_pipeline.quality_impact: No rendering impact. Player-visible quality impact is entirely about update experience: patch size, update duration, and disk space consumed during a rebuild.
differential_patch_pipeline.concept_impact: Determines the feasible content cadence. A pipeline with bad patch behaviour cannot ship small frequent updates, which in turn constrains live-ops and content drops more than any production capacity limit.
differential_patch_pipeline.recommended_stage: production setup, before the first external build - the pack layout cannot be changed later without invalidating every already-shipped patch.

relations.note: Install size is what the first download costs; patch size is what every subsequent one costs. Both are decided by the same pack layout.
Streaming units and downloadable units are not the same thing; if chunk assignment follows the wrong one, a small content change invalidates a large download.
Reordering assets to improve load order is a patch-size regression; the two optimisations directly conflict and must be traded off explicitly.
Re-encoding every mesh in a build changes the bytes of every mesh, which defeats chunk matching even though almost nothing changed visually.
Both are about the cost of moving bytes from disk into the game; one optimises the first delivery, the other the per-load path.

differential_patch_pipeline.verification: The decisive test is cheap and should be run on every release candidate: take the previous live build, make one small representative content change, build, and read the reported update size. If it is not close to the size of the change, diff the pack files with a binary diff tool and confirm 'that the differences shown are of the size you expect for the changed assets, and that there aren't perhaps dozens or hundreds of small changes spread out throughout the file'. Also verify the local rebuild cost on a minimum-spec drive.

claims.statement: 'Each file is scanned and divided into small chunks of about 1MB. If the depot has been built before, this partitioning will preserve as many of the unchanged chunks as possible... New file chunks are compressed, encrypted, and then uploaded to the MDS.'

'SteamPipe has an efficient patching algorithm based on binary deltas, only changing the modified portions of existing content files. When this content is updated, only these deltas need to be sent.' No numeric compression ratio or average patch-size percentage is published in the documentation.

The documented worst case: with TOC information distributed through the file and stored as absolute byte offsets, 'if an asset at byte 3450 increases in size by 8 bytes, then the offset values for all assets after this in the file change... a change to an 8-byte number will result in a new 1MB chunk being created by SteamPipe. This can have catastrophic effects where even changing a few small assets in a pack file results in clients needing to download over half the entire file to update.'

'SteamPipe does not know about asset boundaries within a pack file. If sub-megabyte assets are shuffled, it will most likely not be able to detect this reordering as the previously determined 1-MB chunks will no longer be present within the file.'

'If, in the process of creating an update for your game, you wish to optimize load times by reordering assets within the pack file, be cognizant of the fact that it may result in a very large download for that update. We recommend only doing this if the performance improvements are significant.'

'You should ensure that compression is per-asset as much as possible. Any compression that crosses asset boundaries will spread out changes and require clients to download more data than necessary.' The same risk is stated for encryption.

'A final manifest is generated for this depot version; each manifest is identified by a unique 64-bit manifest ID.' Preload updates are 'delivered as a delta patch from the previous build in the same way they are after release' but are encrypted and not applied until release, so 'multiple large updates can end up consuming a large amount of space on-disk'.

The Steamworks documentation publishes no average or typical patch-size percentage; the only size language is the qualitative worst case ('over half the entire file'). I found no shipped-title patch-size statistic in the sources I could verify.

directstorage_io.problem: Traditional file IO wastes fast storage. Games issue huge numbers of small reads, and the per-request CPU overhead - not the device - becomes the limit long before an NVMe SSD is saturated, so loading a streamed world costs CPU time and latency rather than bandwidth. DirectStorage replaces the per-read syscall-and-copy model with a batched queue of requests that complete through fences, optionally decompressed by the GPU, so that the limiting factor becomes the device rather than the CPU.

implementation_variants.name: Batched read queue, no compression
implementation_variants.description: The base pattern: create a queue, enqueue many requests at once, and wait on a fence rather than polling per request. This alone is the change - 'minimal CPU overhead' for many small reads comes from batching and from not blocking per read.

implementation_variants.name: GDeflate compressed reads with CPU decompression
implementation_variants.description: Store assets compressed and decompress on the CPU inside the DirectStorage pipeline. GDeflate is designed for the GPU case but decodes on the CPU too: it is 'designed to allow for concurrent decoding of symbols from different sub-streams in a bulk-synchronous ...' fashion, which is what makes parallel decode possible.

implementation_variants.name: GPU decompression
implementation_variants.description: Have the GPU do the decompression so the CPU never touches the bytes. This was explicitly roadmap at the 1.0 announcement - 'GPU decompression is next on our roadmap, a feature that will give developers more control over resources and how hardware is leveraged' - and it is what the GpuDecompressionBenchmark sample exists to compare against CPU decompression.

implementation_variants.name: Staging buffer size tuning
implementation_variants.description: Staging buffer size is a real tuning parameter with a measurable effect: the benchmark sample was added 'to measure performance and demonstrate the effects of varying staging buffer sizes', and it exposes chunk size ('defaults to 256 KiB; adjustable via -chunksize') and a sustained-throughput mode that 'better reflects real-world loading scenarios where many requests are in flight'.

implementation_variants.name: Keep a conventional IO fallback path
implementation_variants.description: Microsoft's own guidance is conditional on the device: 'While you may see benefits on any kind of storage device, installing games to an NVMe SSD will maximize your IO performance', and Windows 11 is 'our recommended path for gaming'. A game shipping to HDDs and SATA SSDs needs the old path to remain correct and reasonably fast. This is engineering judgement; the conditional benefit is documented.

implementation_variants.name: Pair it with an async loading layer that can actually feed it
implementation_variants.description: A fast IO path only helps if something is issuing enough requests to keep it busy. Unreal's async loading (soft references plus FStreamableManager::RequestAsyncLoad) is that layer on the engine side; without a request stream, batching has nothing to batch.

directstorage_io.applicability_conditions: Windows titles whose load or streaming time is limited by IO request overhead rather than by raw bandwidth - most obviously open worlds with continuous streaming and large numbers of small asset reads. The benefit is device-dependent and Microsoft's own framing is conditional (NVMe, Windows 11 recommended).
directstorage_io.limitations: The decisive honest caveat: I could not find a published measured throughput or load-time figure from Microsoft. The documentation defines the goal ('multiple gigabytes a second of small (for example, 64kb) data reads with minimal CPU overhead') but the repository ships a benchmark harness rather than results - 'results are automatically copied to the clipboard' for the user to paste into a spreadsheet - so any GB/s number must be produced on the target hardware. Benefit is conditional on storage device and OS. Adoption also means owning a second IO path for platforms or devices where DirectStorage is not available or not beneficial.
directstorage_io.required_data_and_tools: The DirectStorage SDK, a compression format compatible with the decompression path (GDeflate), a request-generation layer that can keep the queue fed, and - necessarily - a measurement harness run on the minimum-spec target device.

impact.cpu: high positive intended - 'minimal CPU overhead' per read is the entire point; the saving is CPU time, not bandwidth
impact.gpu: low to medium negative if GPU decompression is used (it moves work to the GPU, during load or streaming)
impact.ram: low - staging buffers, sized as a tuning parameter (sample default 256 KiB chunks)
impact.vram: low - destination buffers and decompression scratch
impact.disk: neutral to positive - enables storing more data compressed, since decompression is cheaper or offloaded
impact.network: none

directstorage_io.quality_impact: Load times and streaming responsiveness; no rendering quality impact. The quality risk is a stall when the queue is not kept fed, which turns into a hitch or a missing asset at the streaming boundary.
directstorage_io.concept_impact: Raises the ceiling on how much world can be streamed, which is what makes higher asset density and larger streaming radii affordable on PC. It is an enabler for other methods in this pack, not a visible feature.
directstorage_io.recommended_stage: production, once the streaming/loading architecture exists and there is something to feed the queue - not before, because the win depends entirely on request volume and device.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3d queue/request/fence integration on the existing load path + 2d GDeflate compression in the cook pipeline + 3d measurement harness and sustained-throughput runs on minimum-spec devices + 2d staging buffer and chunk size tuning; p80 adds GPU decompression, a fallback path for non-NVMe devices and per-title tuning

relations.note: DirectStorage only pays off if the loading layer can keep many requests in flight; the two must be designed together.
Cheaper decompression changes the tradeoff between storing assets compressed and reading them raw, which is an install-size decision as much as a load-time one.
Virtual texture page reads are the archetypal small-read workload: many tiny, latency-sensitive requests, which is exactly the pattern this API targets.
When a streamed or generated world is IO-bound, the achievable bytes per second is the ceiling on the streaming budget.
Both concern moving bytes from disk into the game efficiently; one optimises the delivery, the other the per-load path, and both are affected by how assets are packed and compressed.

directstorage_io.verification: Do not take a number from anyone, including Microsoft: build the GpuDecompressionBenchmark sample, run it on the minimum-spec target device with your own data, and use '-sustained' because 'this better reflects real-world loading scenarios where many requests are in flight'. Compare GPU vs CPU decompression and sweep staging buffer size and chunk size. Then measure the real thing - cold start and worst-case streaming - with and without DirectStorage on the same device, and on an HDD to confirm the fallback path.

claims.statement: 'DirectStorage is a feature intended to allow games to make full use of high-speed storage (such as NVMe SSDs) that can deliver multiple gigabytes a second of small (for example, 64kb) data reads with minimal CPU overhead.'

claims.statement: I found no measured throughput or load-time figure published by Microsoft for DirectStorage. The documentation states the goal but no result; the repository ships a benchmark harness, not benchmark results.
